The X-shaped cross (crux decussata) is traditionally linked with Andrew's martyrdom at Patras. It appears on the flag of Scotland, of which he is patron.
Brothers in two Churches.
Rome honours Peter; Constantinople honours Andrew. Since 1969 the Holy See sends a delegation to Istanbul for 30 November, and the Patriarchate sends one to Rome for 29 June.
The Andrew Christmas novena.
A traditional prayer begins today and is said fifteen times a day until Christmas: “Hail and blessed be the hour and moment in which the Son of God was born of the most pure Virgin Mary…”
Fishers of people.
Jeremiah 16:16 speaks of God sending “many fishermen” to gather his scattered people. Jesus fulfils it in the apostles.
altar: Andrew left his nets; at the altar we leave our cares and offer ourselves with Christ.
Every Mass ends with a mission: “Go forth, the Mass is ended.” Like Andrew, we leave the altar to bring others to the One we have found.
outline: Ask: who first brought you to Jesus? Give thanks for that person.
Andrew follows at once and leaves his nets.
Point 2 · We have found the Messiah
He brings his brother; mission begins at home.
Point 3 · How beautiful are the feet
Faith comes from hearing; someone must speak.
Andrew's X-shaped cross: arms open to the world.
live: Bring one person (John 1:41)
Invite one person to Mass or to an Advent prayer this month.
Begin the St Andrew novena
Pray the St Andrew Christmas prayer daily until Christmas.
Leave a net (Matthew 4:20)
Leave one distraction this Advent to follow Christ more freely.
Pray for unity
Pray for full communion between Catholics and Orthodox.
fathers: St John Chrysostom
He notes that Andrew, after spending just one day with Jesus, ran to share the treasure with his brother: “This is the sign of genuine love.”
St Gregory the Great
He comments that Peter and Andrew left little, a net and a boat, but they left everything, because they left even the desire to possess.
St Bernard of Clairvaux
He imagines Andrew greeting his cross with joy: “O good cross, long desired!”, words from the ancient Passion of Andrew.
magis: “How are they to hear without someone to proclaim him?”: the necessity of being sent.
The Eastern Churches and the search for unity.
saints: 3 Dec: St Francis Xavier, priest, patron of the missions. 4 Dec: First Friday.
2026-11-30.prayer: We humbly implore your majesty, O Lord, that, just as the blessed Apostle Andrew was once a preacher and pastor for your Church, so he may be for us a constant intercessor before you. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

quick: The saints are a multitude no one can count, from every nation.
Holiness is God's grace received, not our achievement.
The Beatitudes are the portrait of a saint.
2026-11-01.action: Thank God by name for three people whose faith formed you.
2026-11-01.question: Which beatitude do I find hardest to live?
2026-11-01.special: Solemnity of All Saints, replacing the Thirty-first Sunday in Ordinary Time.
illus: In many Kerala parishes the cemetery is next to the church. On these days families clean the graves, light candles and pray. Among the names on those stones are surely many saints whom no calendar lists.

family.explain: Jesus tells us how to be truly happy: by being humble, kind, merciful and pure of heart. Saints are people who lived like this.
family.intention: We thank God for the saints in our own family.
family.ask: Ask: “Which beatitude can our family practise this week?”

kidsaint: A poor boy of mixed race in Peru who became a Dominican brother. He swept floors, cared for the sick and fed the poor and even animals. Lesson: you become a saint by doing small things with great love.
term: The Church's solemn declaration that a person is in heaven and may be venerated by the whole Church. It does not make anyone a saint; it recognises what God has done.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you are present wherever two or three gather in your name. On this feast of All Saints we gather as your family on earth, joined to the great multitude in heaven. Send your Holy Spirit to open our hearts to your word, so that we may become the saints you call us to be. Amen.
share: Who is a saint next door in your life, someone whose quiet faith helped you? Share one thing that person did.
Which beatitude do you find hardest to live today, and why? (Matthew 5:3–12)
The saints washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb (Revelation 7:14). What does God's forgiveness mean to you on the road to holiness?
interc: For the Church throughout the world, that she may shine with the holiness of her saints and draw all people to Christ.
For our Pope, our bishop and our priests, that they may lead us by word and example on the way of the Beatitudes.
For those who are poor, grieving, persecuted or hungry for justice, that they may receive the comfort Jesus promised.
For our families, that our homes may be schools of holiness where children learn to pray, to forgive and to serve.
For our beloved dead, that they may soon join the multitude before the throne of the Lamb.
pm.close: God of all holiness, you call us to share the life of your saints. Through the prayers of the Blessed Virgin Mary and all the saints, keep us faithful this week and bring us one day to your eternal home. May the Lord bless us, keep us from all evil and bring us to everlasting life. Amen.

qa: What is a saint?
A person who lived in God's friendship and now shares his life in heaven. Everyone in heaven is a saint, whether or not the Church has canonised that person (CCC 828, 956).
Are all Christians called to be saints?
Yes. All the faithful, in every state of life, are called to the fullness of Christian life and the perfection of charity (Lumen Gentium 40; CCC 2013).
Do Catholics worship the saints?
No. Worship belongs to God alone. We honour the saints as friends of God and ask for their prayers, just as we ask fellow Christians on earth to pray for us (CCC 956–957, 2132).
What is the communion of saints?
The union of all who belong to Christ: the faithful on earth, the souls being purified and the saints in heaven, who share spiritual goods and pray for one another (CCC 946–962).

quick: God is easily found by those who seek him.
Oil cannot be borrowed: no one can pray or love for us.
The Bridegroom comes to take us in, not to catch us out.
2026-11-08.action: Give God the first five minutes of your morning this week.
2026-11-08.question: Is my lamp burning, or only lit for show?
2026-11-08.special: Thirty-second Sunday in Ordinary Time, Year A. The last Sundays of the year turn our attention to the end of time and the coming of Christ.
illus: In many Kerala homes the evening lamp (nilavilakku) is lit at dusk and the family gathers to pray. Someone must remember to buy oil and trim the wick every day. A lamp left empty one evening does not light just because the family is in a hurry.

family.explain: Ten girls waited for a wedding. Five had extra oil for their lamps and five did not. When the bridegroom came, only the ready ones went in. Jesus wants us to be ready by loving him every day.
family.intention: We pray to be always ready to meet Jesus.
family.ask: Ask: “What is the ‘oil’ in our family's lamp?”

kidsaint: A Roman soldier who cut his cloak in half for a freezing beggar. That night he dreamed of Jesus wearing the half-cloak. Lesson: what we do for the poor, we do for Jesus.
term: Greek for “presence” or “arrival”, used of the glorious return of Christ at the end of time (CCC 1001; 1040).

quick: God gives every person a fortune of gifts.
Fear buries talents; trust multiplies them.
Our gifts are meant to reach the poor.
2026-11-15.action: Use one buried talent this month for the parish or the poor.
2026-11-15.question: What have I buried out of fear?
2026-11-15.special: Thirty-third Sunday in Ordinary Time, Year A. World Day of the Poor.
illus: Many Kerala families keep their gold in a bank locker for years. It is safe, but it does nothing. A talent kept in a locker earns no joy. The capable woman of Proverbs is like the mother who turns little into much, and still has something for the beggar at the door.

family.explain: God gave each of us gifts. Two servants used their gifts and doubled them; one hid his out of fear. God wants us to use our gifts with love, especially for the poor.
family.intention: We pray for the poor in our neighbourhood.
family.ask: Ask: “What gift has God given each of us? How can we use it this week?”

kidsaint: A princess who gave bread to the poor and built a hospital. Once, when she was carrying bread to the poor, the bread is said to have turned into roses. Lesson: share what you have with those in need.
term: In the parable, a large sum of money. In Christian language, any gift of nature or grace that God entrusts to us for others.

quick: Christ the King reigns as a shepherd.
At the end we will be judged on love for the least.
His Kingdom grows wherever mercy is chosen.
2026-11-22.action: Do one corporal work of mercy each day this week.
2026-11-22.question: Where did I meet Christ in the least this week, and pass him by?
2026-11-22.special: Solemnity of Our Lord Jesus Christ, King of the Universe. Last Sunday of the liturgical year, Year A.
illus: In many Kerala parishes the Christ the King procession winds through the streets with bands and umbrellas. A beautiful sign. But Matthew 25 says the King's real procession passes through the hospital ward, the lock-up and the migrant workers' camp.

family.explain: Jesus is our King. He said that when we help someone who is hungry, sick or lonely, we are helping him.
family.intention: We pray for the hungry, the sick and prisoners.
family.ask: Ask: “Whom can our family help this week?”

catechism: Christ will come again to judge the living and the dead.
kidsaint: A 14-year-old Mexican boy martyred in 1928. Even under torture he would not deny Jesus, crying “Long live Christ the King!” (Canonised in 2016.) Lesson: Jesus is King of my heart.
term: Christ is King by nature as the Son of God and by right as Redeemer. His Kingdom is “not from this world” (John 18:36) but is present in mystery in the Church and will be completed in glory.

quick: Advent begins with longing: tear open the heavens and come down.
We are the clay; let the Potter reshape us.
Keep awake: Christ comes.
2026-11-29.action: Set up an Advent wreath and pray five minutes as a family each evening.
2026-11-29.question: What am I really waiting for this Christmas?
2026-11-29.special: First Sunday of Advent. New liturgical year, Year B (Mark). Colour: violet.
illus: In Kerala, before a family wedding, the whole house is cleaned, painted and lit days in advance, and someone always waits at the gate to receive the guests. Advent asks: is anyone waiting at the gate of my heart for Christ?

family.explain: Advent means “coming”. We get ready for Jesus' birthday, and we also remember that Jesus will come again. We keep our hearts awake by praying and doing good.
family.intention: We pray that our family may be ready to welcome Jesus.
family.ask: Ask: “What can each of us do this week to get ready for Jesus?”

catechism: Christ will come again in glory.
kidsaint: A fisherman who met Jesus and immediately ran to bring his brother Peter: “We have found the Messiah!” Lesson: when you find Jesus, bring someone else to him.
term: From the Latin for “coming”: the four weeks before Christmas, preparing to celebrate Christ's first coming and looking forward to his second coming.

quick: Our dead are in the hand of God.
Purgatory is God's love completing what was unfinished; our prayers help.
Our final hope is the resurrection.
2026-11-02.action: Visit a grave, or have a Mass offered for your departed.
2026-11-02.question: Whom have I forgotten to pray for?
2026-11-02.special: All Souls. In November the Church prays especially for the faithful departed.
illus: In many Kerala homes there is a framed photo of a departed grandparent with a lamp before it. That lamp is a prayer: we have not forgotten you, and we trust you to God.

family.explain: When someone we love dies, Jesus does not forget them. He promises to raise them up. Our prayers help them reach heaven.
family.intention: We pray for our grandparents and all our departed relatives.

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, today is a family feast. We celebrate not one saint but all of them, the known and the unknown, the great multitude that no one can count.

When we hear the word “saint”, we may think of statues and halos and miracles. But John saw a crowd from every nation, tribe and language. Among them are mothers who prayed the rosary every evening, fathers who worked honestly, children who died young, priests and sisters who served quietly. Some of them are from our own families.

How did they get there? The elder tells John: “they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.” Not by being perfect from the beginning, but by letting Jesus wash them again and again. A saint is a sinner who never stopped coming back to God.

And how does a saint live? Jesus gives us the Beatitudes. Poor in spirit: knowing that I need God. Meek: not proud or violent. Merciful: forgiving. Pure of heart: looking at others without lust or envy. Peacemakers: building bridges in our families and parishes. These are not rules imposed from outside; they are the face of Jesus himself.

St John tells us: “we are God's children now.” We already belong to this family. Holiness is not for a few special people. The Church says that every baptised person is called to holiness. Pope Francis speaks of the “saints next door”, ordinary people who live their faith with love.

So today, let us thank God for the saints who have gone before us, and let us ask them to pray for us. And let us take one step this week: one beatitude, one confession, one act of mercy. The multitude is not yet complete; there is a place for you.
kids: Children, who is a saint? Someone who loves God and others very much.
Saints were children once, like you. They made mistakes, said sorry, and kept trying to be good.
Jesus gave us a list of ways to be happy: be kind, be humble, forgive, make peace.
Today choose one: make peace with a brother or sister or a friend. That is how saints begin!

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, when we hear the word saint we think of statues, haloes and miracles. But today's feast is much bigger than the saints whose names are in the calendar. St John saw a great multitude that no one could count, from every nation, tribe, people and language (Revelation 7:9). Most of them were never canonised. Today is their feast.

Pope Francis speaks of the saints next door: parents who raise their children with love, men and women who work hard to support their families, the sick, elderly religious who never lose their smile (Gaudete et Exsultate 7). Perhaps your grandmother, who prayed the Rosary every evening and forgave those who hurt her, is among that multitude. Perhaps a teacher who never gave up on a difficult pupil.

The Second Vatican Council taught clearly that all the faithful, of whatever state or rank, are called to the fullness of Christian life and the perfection of charity (Lumen Gentium 40). Holiness is not reserved for priests and nuns. It is the vocation of the mother at home, the driver in traffic, the student before an exam.

How? Jesus gives the portrait in the Beatitudes: poor in spirit, meek, merciful, pure in heart, peacemakers (Matthew 5:3–10). Holiness grows in small things: patience at the dinner table, honesty at work, a kind word to someone nobody likes, a quiet prayer in the middle of a busy day. Whoever is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much (Luke 16:10).

So today let us thank God for the saints next door who formed our faith, and let us ask their help. And let us leave this Holy Mass with a simple resolution: to do one ordinary thing this week with extraordinary love. That is how the great multitude was formed, and that is how we can join it.

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, every Sunday in the Creed we say: I believe in the communion of saints. On this solemnity it is good to ask what these words mean, because our Protestant friends sometimes ask us why Catholics pray to the saints.

The Church teaches that the one family of God exists in three conditions: some are pilgrims on earth, some have died and are being purified, and some are in glory contemplating God (CCC 954). All of us belong to the one Body of Christ. Death does not cut us off from one another. The Letter to the Hebrews says that we are surrounded by a great cloud of witnesses (Hebrews 12:1).

Why do we ask the saints to pray for us? For the same reason we ask one another to pray. The saints are close to God and they love us; their intercession is one of the ways they serve God's plan (CCC 956). In the Book of Revelation the elders before the throne hold golden bowls of incense, which are the prayers of the saints (Revelation 5:8). Their prayer does not compete with Christ, the one Mediator; it flows from His love and leads to Him. We honour the saints, but we adore God alone (CCC 2132).

When the Church canonises someone, she declares that this person practised heroic virtue and lived in fidelity to God's grace, and is now with God (CCC 828). The saints show that the Gospel can be lived in every century and every culture: in Rome and in Kerala, in palaces and in slums, in youth and in old age.

So the saints are friends, intercessors and models. St Paul could say: be imitators of me, as I am of Christ (1 Corinthians 11:1). Choose a saint this month as your friend. Read their life. Ask for their prayer every day. And let this Holy Mass, where heaven and earth are joined, renew your desire not only to admire the saints but to become one.
Dear brothers and sisters, every Malayali knows what it is to wait for a wedding procession. Today Jesus tells a story about ten young women waiting for the bridegroom.

All ten were invited. All ten had lamps. And all ten fell asleep, because the bridegroom was late. Jesus does not blame them for sleeping. The difference was simple: five had brought extra oil, and five had not.

At midnight the cry went up: “Look! Here is the bridegroom!” The foolish ones said, “Give us some of your oil.” But the wise could not. Why? Because some things cannot be shared at the last moment. My faith cannot replace yours. My prayer cannot be your prayer. The Fathers said the oil is charity, good works, the life of grace. These are gathered slowly, drop by drop, day by day.

The first reading says Wisdom is easy to find: “she will be found sitting at the gate.” God is not hiding. He is waiting at the door of our day. Those who rise early to seek him find him. So the question is not whether God is available, but whether we go to him.

And St Paul reminds us why we wait with hope and not fear. Some in Thessalonica had lost loved ones. Paul says: do not grieve as those who have no hope. Jesus died and rose, and those who died in him will rise with him, “and so we will be with the Lord forever.” This November, as we pray for our dead, these words are our comfort.

So let us fill our flasks this week. A few minutes of prayer each morning. A Sunday Mass that is never missed. A kindness to someone in need. Drop by drop, the lamp is filled. And when the Bridegroom comes, may he find our lamps burning.
kids: Children, have you ever waited for a guest who was late?
Jesus told a story about ten girls waiting for a bridegroom with lamps. Five brought extra oil, and five forgot.
The oil is like our love for Jesus: we fill it up a little every day when we pray and are kind.
Tonight, before sleeping, say: “Jesus, I love you. Keep my lamp burning!”

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, today Jesus tells the story of a master who entrusts his wealth to his servants. To one he gives five talents, to another two, to another one. Do you know how much a talent was? About twenty years' wages. Even the servant with one talent received a fortune.
That is the first lesson: God is generous with everyone. No one in this church is without gifts. Your life, health, intelligence, faith, family, time, money: all of it is entrusted.

Two servants worked hard and doubled what they received. The master's words to them are beautiful: “Well done, good and trustworthy servant… enter into the joy of your master.” God wants to share his joy with us.

But the third servant buried his talent. Why? He says: “I knew that you were a harsh man… so I was afraid.” He had a wrong picture of God. When we think God is harsh and waiting to punish, we become afraid to try, afraid to serve, afraid to love. Fear buries talents. Trust multiplies them.

The first reading shows us a capable woman. She works with willing hands, and “she opens her hand to the poor.” Today is the World Day of the Poor. Our talents are not only for our own success; they are meant to reach the poor, the lonely, the sick.

So let us ask this week: what have I buried? Perhaps a gift of music, teaching, organising, listening, or simply time. Dig it up and use it. And let us open our hands to the poor, not only with money but with our presence. Then one day we too will hear: “Well done… enter into the joy of your master.”
kids: Children, God has given each of you special gifts. Can you name one? Singing, drawing, running, being kind?
Jesus told a story about servants who were given money. Two used it well; one hid it in the ground because he was afraid.
God doesn't want us to hide our gifts. He wants us to use them to help others.
This week, use one of your gifts to make someone happy!

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, today we end the Church year by crowning Christ as King. But what kind of King is he?

The prophet Ezekiel tells us: God says, “I myself will search for my sheep… I will seek the lost, bring back the strayed, bind up the injured, strengthen the weak.” Our King is a Shepherd. He does not rule by fear; he rules by care.

In the Gospel we see this King at the end of time, seated on his glorious throne, with all the nations before him. And what will he ask us? Not how much money we earned, not how many titles we held, not even how many devotions we attended. He will ask: “I was hungry, did you feed me? I was a stranger, did you welcome me? I was sick, did you visit me? I was in prison, did you come to me?”

And both groups are surprised: “Lord, when did we see you?” The King answers: “Just as you did it to one of the least of these, you did it to me.” Christ hides himself in the poor. St John Chrysostom said: do not honour Christ in church with silk while you neglect him outside, naked and cold.

St Paul tells us that Christ must reign until every enemy is defeated, and the last enemy is death. Then God will be all in all. That is where history is going. Every act of mercy, every plate of food shared, every visit to a lonely person, is a step in that direction: a small crowning of Christ.

So this last week of the year, let us choose one work of mercy each day. And when we say in the Our Father, “Thy Kingdom come,” let us mean it with our hands as well as our lips. Long live Christ the King!
kids: Children, what does a king wear? A crown! Jesus is our King, but his crown was made of thorns.
Jesus said that when we help a poor or sick person, we are helping him.
He is a King who looks after people like a shepherd looks after his sheep.
This week, help one person: share your snack, visit a sick grandparent, be kind to a new classmate. That's how we crown Jesus!

intro: Today we crown Christ as King. But His crown was made of thorns and His throne was a cross.

opts.resolve: This week I will let Christ reign in one area of my life that I have kept for myself.
homily: Dear brothers and sisters, on this last Sunday of the liturgical year we proclaim Christ as King of the universe. We sing, we crown His image, we carry Him in procession. But let us remember what kind of crown He wore on earth: a crown of thorns.

When Pilate asked Jesus whether He was a king, Jesus answered: my kingdom is not from this world. He came to testify to the truth, and everyone who belongs to the truth listens to His voice (John 18:36–37). Pilate had soldiers, a palace and the power of Rome. Jesus had nothing but truth and love. Yet two thousand years later Pilate is remembered only because his name is in our Creed, and Jesus reigns in the hearts of millions.

Above the Cross the soldiers nailed an inscription: this is the King of the Jews (Luke 23:38). They meant it as a mockery, but it was the truth. Christ reigns from the Cross. His power is not to take life but to give it. And the first one to recognise His kingship was a dying criminal who said: Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom. Jesus answered: today you will be with me in Paradise (Luke 23:42–43).

So the real question today is not whether Christ is King of the universe. He is, whether the world accepts it or not. The question is whether He is King of my heart. Does He reign over my tongue, my money, my phone, my family, my work, my politics? Or have I kept some area of my life closed to Him, a little kingdom of my own?

As we end this liturgical year, let us open every door to Christ. Let us serve as He served, especially the least of His brothers and sisters. And when we receive Him in this Holy Mass, let us say with the good thief: Jesus, remember me in your kingdom. That prayer is enough to save a whole life.

opts.a: Teaching homily: the Kingship of Christ in the Church's teaching
intro: Pope Pius XI established this feast in 1925 (Quas Primas), when nations were turning away from God. Its message is even more urgent today.

sub: By nature: He is the Son of God (Colossians 1:15–17).
By conquest: He redeemed us by His blood (1 Peter 1:18–19).

concl: Christ's Kingship is the foundation of our hope and our mission.
Every Christian shares His royal office by serving.
opts.resolve: This week I will pray Thy kingdom come with attention and do one act of justice.
homily: Dear brothers and sisters, this feast is younger than many of us think. Pope Pius XI established it in 1925, in the encyclical Quas Primas. Europe had just come out of a terrible war, ideologies were rising that put the State or the race in the place of God, and many nations were living as if God did not exist. The Pope proclaimed: Christ is King, of individuals, of families and of societies.

Why is Christ King? First, by His very nature: He is the eternal Son of God, through whom and for whom all things were created (Colossians 1:15–17). Second, by conquest: He redeemed us, not with silver or gold, but with His precious blood (1 Peter 1:18–19). Third, because the Father has given Him all authority in heaven and on earth (Matthew 28:18). Daniel saw one like a son of man receiving an everlasting dominion (Daniel 7:13–14).

His Kingdom is already present and not yet complete. The Second Vatican Council says that the Church is the Kingdom of Christ already present in mystery (Lumen Gentium 3). It grows quietly like a mustard seed. But it will be fulfilled only when Christ comes again in glory, when He hands over the Kingdom to the Father and God will be all in all (1 Corinthians 15:24–28; CCC 671). Until then we pray every day: Thy kingdom come.

Does this feast have anything to say to society? Yes. The Catechism teaches that Christians have the duty to bring the spirit of the Gospel into the life of society, its customs, laws and structures (CCC 2105). That means defending the dignity of every human life from conception to natural death, working for justice and peace, caring for the poor and the migrant. It does not mean forcing faith on anyone; the Church respects freedom of conscience. We propose Christ by our witness.

Through Baptism we share in Christ's royal office, which means to serve (CCC 786). The King washed feet. So let us end this liturgical year by renewing our allegiance to Christ, and let us show it by serving the least of His brothers and sisters. Then His Kingdom will come, a little more, in our homes and in our land.
Dear brothers and sisters, today we begin a new Church year. We light the first candle on the Advent wreath. A small flame in the dark, but it says: someone is coming.

The first reading is a prayer from people who were tired and disappointed. They had come back from exile, but life was hard and they felt far from God. And they cried out: “O that you would tear open the heavens and come down!” Do we ever pray like that? For our families, for our nation, for the world?

They were honest about their sins. But they held on to one truth: “Yet, O Lord, you are our Father; we are the clay, and you are the potter.” That is Advent: we bring our broken clay to the Potter and ask him to shape us again.
And God answered. He did tear open the heavens. He came down at Bethlehem, as a child. And he will come again in glory. Advent prepares us for both comings.

In the Gospel Jesus gives one word, repeated: “Keep awake.” He mentions evening, midnight, cockcrow and dawn. Those were the hours of his own Passion night, when the disciples kept falling asleep. Jesus asks us to stay awake with him: through prayer, through honesty, through charity.

So let us use these four weeks well. Set up the Advent wreath at home and pray together each evening. Make a good Confession early. Choose one habit you want God to reshape. Then Christmas will not be just a holiday, but a meeting with the One who comes.
kids: Children, what is this circle of green with candles? It's an Advent wreath!
Each Sunday we light one more candle. When all four are lit, it will be almost Christmas!
Advent means “coming”. Jesus is coming! We get ready by praying and being kind.
At home, light a candle every evening and say: “Come, Lord Jesus!”

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, yesterday we celebrated the saints in heaven. Today we pray for all who have died, especially our own families: parents, grandparents, brothers and sisters, friends.

Death is painful. Even Jesus wept at the grave of Lazarus. The Church does not ask us to hide our grief. But she gives us a hope that changes it. The Book of Wisdom says: “The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God.” Our dead are not lost; they are held.

Why do we pray for them? Because many of us die not yet fully ready to see God face to face. The Church teaches that there is a final purification, Purgatory. It is not a place of despair but of hope; those there are certain of heaven. It is like gold refined in the fire. And our love can help them: our prayers, our sacrifices, and above all the Holy Mass.
St Monica, dying far from home, said to her son Augustine: “Lay this body anywhere. Only this I ask: remember me at the altar of the Lord.” That is what we do today. We bring our dead to the altar.

And Jesus gives us his promise: “This is the will of my Father, that all who see the Son and believe in him may have eternal life; and I will raise them up on the last day.” Our faith is not only that the soul lives on. We believe in the resurrection of the body. The graves we visit are resting places, waiting for that morning.

So this week, visit the cemetery, light a candle, pray the rosary for the dead, and have a Mass offered. And let us also live in such a way that we are ready when our time comes. Eternal rest grant unto them, O Lord, and let perpetual light shine upon them.
kids: Children, do you remember someone in your family who has died?
Jesus loves them, and they are with God. Some of them may need our prayers to be fully ready for heaven.
We can help them by praying: “Eternal rest grant unto them, O Lord.”
Let's say this prayer every night this month for our grandparents and all who have died.

opts.a: A month of remembering: love that becomes prayer
intro: November is the month of the holy souls. Today we visit graves, light candles and offer the Holy Mass for our dead.

sub: Our dead gave us life, faith, love.
Gratitude heals grief.
Tell their stories to the children.
points.apply: Write down three things you received from a loved one who has died.

sub: Death is not the end.
God wills that none be lost (John 6:39).
Our prayer helps those being purified.
points.apply: Have the Holy Mass offered for your dead this month.

sub: Every grave preaches a sermon.
Reconcile, confess, make peace.
Live so as to die well.
points.apply: Make a good confession this month.

concl: Remembering, praying, preparing: three ways love goes on.
Our cemeteries are not places of despair but of waiting.
opts.resolve: This month I will pray for my dead every day and make my own peace with God.
homily: Dear brothers and sisters, today our cemeteries are full of flowers and candles. Families come to clean the graves, to pray and to remember. The whole month of November is dedicated to the holy souls. Today let us think about three things we do for our dead: we remember, we pray and we prepare.

First, we remember with gratitude. Our parents, grandparents, brothers and sisters, friends and priests who have died gave us so much: life itself, the faith, love, sacrifices we may never know. St Paul wrote that he thanked God every time he remembered his friends (Philippians 1:3). Gratitude heals grief. Tell their stories to your children, so that the next generation knows where its faith came from.

Second, we pray with hope. The Book of Wisdom says that the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God (Wisdom 3:1). Jesus said that it is the will of the Father that He should lose nothing of all that has been given Him, but raise it up on the last day (John 6:39). Those who have died in God's friendship but are not yet fully purified can be helped by our prayers, especially by the Holy Mass. So have the Holy Mass offered for your dead, pray the Rosary for them, give alms in their name.

Third, we prepare our own departure. Every grave preaches a silent sermon: one day it will be my turn. The psalm prays: teach us to count our days, that we may gain a wise heart (Psalm 90:12). Do not wait to make peace with God and with others. Make a good confession this month. Forgive the person you have not forgiven.

Then our cemeteries will not be places of despair, but places of waiting, gardens where seeds have been sown for the resurrection. Eternal rest grant unto them, O Lord, and let perpetual light shine upon them.

opts.a: Teaching homily: purgatory, indulgences and prayer for the dead
intro: Many Catholics are unsure what the Church teaches about purgatory and indulgences. Today is the right day to explain.

sub: A final purification for those who die in God's grace but imperfectly purified (CCC 1030–1031).
Not a second chance, but the completion of love.
A fire of love, not of punishment only.
points.apply: Thank God that His mercy finishes what we leave unfinished.

points.h: How we help the holy souls
sub: The Holy Mass offered for them (CCC 1032, 1371).
Prayer, almsgiving, works of penance.
Indulgences applied to the dead (CCC 1479).
points.apply: Offer one sacrifice each week of November for a soul.

sub: Remission of temporal punishment due to forgiven sins (CCC 1471).
Conditions: confession, Communion, prayer for the Pope's intentions, detachment from sin.
In the first days of November, a plenary indulgence for the dead may be gained by visiting a cemetery and praying.
points.apply: Gain an indulgence for a deceased family member this week.

concl: Prayer for the dead is an ancient practice of the Church and an act of mercy.
The Church's teaching is full of hope: God's love purifies and saves.
opts.resolve: This week I will go to confession and gain an indulgence for one of my dead.
homily: Dear brothers and sisters, on All Souls' Day it is good to understand clearly what the Church teaches, because there is much confusion about purgatory and indulgences.

The Catechism says that all who die in God's grace and friendship, but still imperfectly purified, are indeed assured of their eternal salvation; but after death they undergo purification, so as to achieve the holiness necessary to enter the joy of heaven. The Church gives the name purgatory to this final purification (CCC 1030–1031). It is not a second chance for those who rejected God, and it is not hell. It is the completion of love, the fire of God's love burning away what is still selfish in us. St Paul speaks of a person being saved, but only as through fire (1 Corinthians 3:15).

From the beginning the Church has honoured the memory of the dead and offered prayers for them. Judas Maccabeus made atonement for the dead, that they might be delivered from their sin (2 Maccabees 12:46). Above all the Church offers the Eucharistic sacrifice for them, and also commends almsgiving, indulgences and works of penance (CCC 1032).

What is an indulgence? When our sins are forgiven in confession, the guilt is taken away, but there can remain what the Church calls temporal punishment, the wounds and disorder that sin leaves. An indulgence is a remission of that temporal punishment, granted through the Church from the treasury of the merits of Christ and the saints (CCC 1471, 1476–1477). Indulgences can be applied to the dead (CCC 1479). The usual conditions are sacramental confession, Holy Communion, prayer for the intentions of the Pope, and detachment from all sin. In the first days of November the Church grants a plenary indulgence, applicable to the dead, to those who visit a cemetery and pray for the departed.

So this is not a dry doctrine; it is a work of mercy. Our dead cannot help themselves, but we can help them. Go to confession this week, receive Communion, visit the cemetery and pray for your dead. And may the souls of the faithful departed, through the mercy of God, rest in peace.

Dear friends, the Sadducees, who denied the resurrection, try to make it look absurd with a story of seven brothers who each married the same woman. Whose wife will she be? Jesus answers that the risen life is not a copy of this one: those who rise cannot die any more, because they are like angels and are children of God, being children of the resurrection (Luke 20:35–36).

Then he answers from the Torah they accepted: at the burning bush God called himself the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob, long after they had died. He is God not of the dead but of the living, for to him all of them are alive (Luke 20:37–38).

In the first reading two witnesses are killed, and after three and a half days the breath of life from God enters them and they stand on their feet (Revelation 11:11). Death does not have the last word over God's witnesses.

Today we celebrate the Presentation of the Blessed Virgin Mary. An ancient tradition tells that Mary was offered to God in the Temple as a child. Her whole life was given to the God of the living. Let us give him our day, and pray the Angelus this week, joining Mary's yes. Amen.
kids: Children, today we remember little Mary being given to God. She said yes to God all her life. Say the Hail Mary today and give your day to God like her.

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, today the whole Church celebrates the birthday of a church building in Rome: the Basilica of St John Lateran. Why? Because it is the Pope's cathedral, “the mother and head of all churches”. To celebrate it is to celebrate our unity with Peter's successor.

Ezekiel saw a river flowing from the Temple. It started small and became deep, and wherever it flowed, everything lived; even the salty Dead Sea became fresh. That is what the Church is meant to be: a source of life flowing out into the world.

In the Gospel Jesus makes a whip and drives out the sellers. He is not against worship; he is against turning God's house into a market. Then he says something astonishing: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” He was speaking of his body. The true Temple is Jesus himself.

St Paul then says to us: “You are God's temple, and God's Spirit dwells in you.” Every baptised person is a temple. So we must ask: what is being sold in my temple? Greed, impurity, anger, gossip? Jesus wants to cleanse us too, not to punish but to make room for God.

Let us love our churches, keep them holy and silent, and come early to pray. Let us pray for the Pope and our bishop. And let us allow the river of grace to flow through us to others, so that wherever we go, life may grow.
kids: Children, whose house is the church? God's house!
Jesus loved his Father's house so much that he chased out people who were selling things there.
Do you know you are also God's house? The Holy Spirit lives in you!
Let's keep our hearts clean and our church quiet and beautiful for Jesus.

opts.a: Living stones: we are the temple
intro: A church in Rome is celebrated everywhere because it is the Pope's cathedral, mother of all churches. But St Paul reminds us that we too are God's temple.

sub: You are God's building (1 Corinthians 3:9).
Christ is the foundation.
Each of us is a stone, placed by God.
points.apply: Ask: what kind of stone am I in my parish?

sub: The Spirit dwells in you (1 Corinthians 3:16).
Respect for the body and for others.
Sin defiles the temple.
points.apply: Make a good confession to cleanse the temple.

sub: Jesus drove out the traders (John 2:13–22).
What clutters our hearts and our churches?
Zeal for God's house.
points.apply: Remove one thing that distracts you from prayer.

concl: We celebrate a building because it points to the people who are God's temple.
Unity with the Pope and the universal Church is part of our faith.
opts.resolve: This week I will pray for the Pope and remove one thing that clutters my heart.
homily: Dear brothers and sisters, why does the whole Church celebrate the dedication of a basilica in Rome? Because St John Lateran is the cathedral of the Bishop of Rome, the Pope. Its inscription calls it the mother and head of all the churches of the city and of the world. Today's feast is a sign of our unity with the Successor of Peter.

But St Paul takes us further. You are God's building, he says, and no one can lay any foundation other than the one that has been laid, Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 3:9–11). The real temple of God is not made of marble. It is made of people. Each of us is a stone placed by God in His building. Some stones are visible, some hidden in the foundations; all are necessary.

Then Paul asks a startling question: do you not know that you are God's temple and that God's Spirit dwells in you? (1 Corinthians 3:16). Since Baptism, the Holy Spirit lives in us. That gives our bodies a great dignity and calls for respect: for our own body, for the bodies of others, for the poor and the sick. Sin defiles the temple; confession cleanses it.

In the Gospel Jesus enters the Temple and drives out the traders with a whip of cords (John 2:13–17). The disciples remembered the psalm: zeal for your house will consume me. What clutters the temple of our hearts? Greed, resentment, screens that leave no room for prayer, gossip. And what clutters our parishes? Divisions, pride, business without prayer. Let Jesus cleanse His house.

Ezekiel saw water flowing from the Temple, bringing life wherever it went (Ezekiel 47:1–12). When the Church is clean and united, grace flows from it into the world. Today let us pray for the Pope and for unity in the Church, and let us offer ourselves as living stones in the house of God.

opts.a: Teaching homily: why church buildings matter
intro: Catholics sometimes ask: if God is everywhere, why do we need churches? Today's feast gives the answer.

points.h: God chose to dwell among us
sub: From the tent of meeting to the Temple.
In Christ, God's dwelling with us (John 1:14).
The church building as a sign (CCC 1179–1180).
points.apply: Visit a church this week just to pray.

sub: The altar, place of sacrifice (CCC 1182).
The tabernacle, Christ's presence (CCC 1183).
The ambo, the font, the confessional (CCC 1184–1185).
points.apply: Genuflect with faith before the tabernacle.

sub: The rite of dedication: anointing of the altar and walls.
Respect: silence, dress, conduct.
The cathedral as sign of unity with the bishop and the Pope.
points.apply: Keep silence in church before and after the Holy Mass.

concl: Church buildings express our faith and help us pray.
The visible church points to the living Church, and to the heavenly Jerusalem.
opts.resolve: I will keep silence in church and genuflect with faith before the tabernacle.
homily: Dear brothers and sisters, some people say: God is everywhere, so why do we need churches? I can pray at home or under a tree. It is true that God is everywhere, and that we can pray anywhere. But today's feast reminds us why church buildings matter.

From the beginning God chose to dwell among His people in a special way: the tent of meeting in the desert, then the Temple in Jerusalem. Solomon himself admitted that the highest heaven cannot contain God, much less a house built by human hands, yet he asked God to keep His eyes open toward that house night and day (1 Kings 8:27–30). In Christ, God's dwelling with us became a person: the Word became flesh and lived among us (John 1:14). The church building is a sign of that presence and of the Church, the people gathered by God (CCC 1179–1180).

A Catholic church is first of all the house of the Eucharist. The altar is the place where the sacrifice of the Cross is made present and the table of the Lord to which the people are invited (CCC 1182). The tabernacle holds the Blessed Sacrament, Christ truly present, for the sick and for adoration (CCC 1183). The ambo is the place of the Word; the baptismal font, the place of new birth; the confessional, the place of mercy (CCC 1184–1185). Every part of the building teaches the faith.

When a church is dedicated, the bishop anoints the altar and the walls with chrism, just as a Christian is anointed. That is why we treat the church with respect: we keep silence, dress modestly, genuflect before the tabernacle, and do not use the church as a social hall.

The Lateran Basilica, the Pope's cathedral, reminds us that every parish church is united to the bishop's cathedral, and every cathedral to Rome. And every church on earth points beyond itself to the heavenly Jerusalem. So love your parish church. Visit it during the week, even for five minutes. Kneel before the tabernacle. There, as nowhere else, Christ waits for you.

Dear brothers and sisters, on the second day of Advent we celebrate St Andrew, the brother of Peter. The Eastern Church calls him “the First-Called”, because he was among the first two to follow Jesus.

What did Andrew do after spending one day with Jesus? He ran to find his brother and said: “We have found the Messiah!” And he brought him to Jesus. That brother became St Peter. Without Andrew's invitation, would there have been a Peter?
Later, it was Andrew who brought the boy with five loaves and two fish. It was Andrew who brought the Greeks who wanted to see Jesus. Andrew is the saint of bringing people.

St Paul tells us why that matters: “How are they to believe in one of whom they have never heard? And how are they to hear without someone to proclaim him?” Faith is passed from person to person. Someone brought you. Who will you bring?

In the Gospel Jesus calls Andrew and Peter from their nets: “Follow me, and I will make you fish for people.” And immediately they left their nets. This Advent, what net is holding us? Too much phone, too much work, an old resentment? Leave it, and follow.
Tradition says Andrew died on an X-shaped cross, greeting it with joy. Today let us thank God for the people who brought us to faith, and let us invite one person this Advent to come and see.
kids: Children, St Andrew was a fisherman. One day he met Jesus and was so happy!
Do you know what he did? He ran to his brother and said: “I found Jesus! Come and see!”
Andrew teaches us to share Jesus with our friends and family.
This week, invite a friend to pray with you or come to church!

opts.a: Andrew, who brought others to Jesus
intro: Every time we meet Andrew in the Gospel, he is bringing someone to Jesus.

sub: We have found the Messiah (John 1:41).
Peter, the rock, was brought by Andrew.
Evangelisation starts at home.
points.apply: Pray for one family member far from faith.

points.h: He brought a boy with five loaves
sub: There is a boy here (John 6:8–9).
Andrew noticed the small gift.
Christ multiplies what we bring.
points.apply: Offer your small gift to the parish.

sub: Some Greeks wished to see Jesus (John 12:20–22).
Andrew opened the door to the nations.
Tradition: he preached widely and was martyred.
points.apply: Invite someone to the Holy Mass this Advent.

concl: Andrew's greatness is that he always pointed away from himself to Christ.
Every Christian is called to bring someone to Jesus.
opts.resolve: This Advent I will invite one person to come with me to the Holy Mass.
homily: Dear brothers and sisters, St Andrew is not as famous as his brother Peter. He did not write letters, and we know few of his words. But whenever we meet him in the Gospel of John, he is doing the same thing: bringing someone to Jesus.

The first time, he brings his own brother. Andrew had spent an afternoon with Jesus, and the first thing he did was to find Simon and tell him: we have found the Messiah. And he brought him to Jesus (John 1:41–42). Think of it: the rock on which Christ built His Church was brought to Christ by Andrew. Evangelisation begins at home, with brothers and sisters, parents and children.

The second time, at the feeding of the five thousand, Andrew brings a boy: there is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish. But what are they among so many? (John 6:8–9). Andrew noticed the small gift that others overlooked. Jesus took those loaves and fed the crowd. Never think your gift is too small. Bring it to Christ and let Him multiply it.

The third time, some Greeks come to Philip saying: sir, we wish to see Jesus. Philip goes to Andrew, and together they bring them to Jesus (John 12:20–22). Andrew opens the door to the nations. Tradition says that he preached the Gospel in many lands and died on a cross, embracing it as a long-desired friend.

On this second day of Advent, Andrew gives us a simple programme. Bring someone to Jesus: a family member who has drifted away, a lonely neighbour, a child who has stopped praying. You do not need to be eloquent. Like Andrew, you need only to say: come and see. Invite one person to the Holy Mass this Advent.

opts.a: Teaching homily: the apostles and apostolic succession
intro: Andrew was one of the Twelve. Today let us understand why the apostles matter for the Church today.

sub: Jesus chose twelve to be with Him and to be sent (Mark 3:14).
The Twelve as foundation of the new Israel.
Andrew, the First-Called.
points.apply: Thank God for the faith that reached you through the apostles.

sub: Faith comes from what is heard (Romans 10:17).
How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news.
Every Christian shares the mission.
points.apply: Speak of your faith simply to one person.

sub: Bishops succeed the apostles (CCC 861–862).
Unity of faith guaranteed.
Andrew honoured as founder by the Church of Constantinople; ecumenism.
points.apply: Pray for Christian unity, especially with the Orthodox Churches.

concl: The Church is apostolic: founded on the apostles, keeping their teaching, guided by their successors.
Andrew links East and West; his feast is a call to unity.
opts.resolve: Today I will pray for unity between the Catholic and Orthodox Churches.
homily: Dear brothers and sisters, in the Creed we confess that the Church is apostolic. On the feast of an apostle it is good to understand what this means.

Jesus chose twelve men to be with Him and to be sent out to proclaim the message (Mark 3:14). They were ordinary men, fishermen like Andrew and Peter, whom He called from their nets (Matthew 4:18–22). The number twelve recalls the twelve tribes: the apostles are the foundation of the new people of God.

St Paul says that faith comes from what is heard, and what is heard comes through the word of Christ; how beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news (Romans 10:15–17). The faith reached us through a chain of witnesses going back to the apostles. In Kerala we gratefully remember St Thomas; in Greece and around the Black Sea, people remember Andrew.

The Church is apostolic in three ways: she is built on the foundation of the apostles; she keeps and hands on their teaching; and she continues to be taught, sanctified and guided by the apostles through their successors, the bishops, in union with the successor of Peter (CCC 857, 861–862). This is why we can be sure that the faith we receive today is the faith of the apostles.

Andrew is also a bridge. The Church of Constantinople honours him as its founder, just as Rome honours Peter. Every year on this day a delegation from Rome visits the Ecumenical Patriarch. Peter and Andrew were brothers; their Churches are sister Churches, still not in full communion. Let us pray today, at this Holy Mass, that the brothers may be fully reunited, and that we may be faithful to the faith of the apostles.

Dear friends, St Paul gives us today one of the oldest hymns of the Church. Christ Jesus, though he was God, did not cling to his glory; he emptied himself, took the form of a slave and became obedient even to death on a cross (Philippians 2:6–8). God's way goes down before it goes up.

Paul does not give us this hymn only to admire it. He begins with a command: let the same mind be in you that was in Christ Jesus (Philippians 2:5). The question for today is simple: where am I clinging to my rights, my place, my image?

In the Gospel a man gives a great banquet. Everything is ready, but the invited guests make excuses: a field, some oxen, a marriage. So the master sends his servant into the streets to bring in the poor, the crippled, the blind and the lame (Luke 14:21). The table of God is full of people the world overlooks.
Every Mass is that banquet. Let us not be among those with excuses. Come to the table this week, even on a weekday if you can, and bring someone with you who feels unwanted. Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus is God, but he came down to be a servant. He invites everyone to his feast, especially the poor. Let us say yes when he invites us to Mass!

homily: Dear friends, large crowds were following Jesus, and he turned and spoke plainly: whoever does not carry the cross and follow me cannot be my disciple (Luke 14:27). He does not want admirers; he wants disciples who know what it costs.

Two short pictures make the point. A man about to build a tower first sits down and counts the cost. A king about to go to war first sits down and considers whether he can win (Luke 14:28–31). Faith is not a sudden feeling; it is a decision taken with open eyes.

Paul tells the Philippians to work out their salvation with fear and trembling, because it is God who is at work in them, and to shine like stars in a crooked world (Philippians 2:12–15). We count the cost, but the strength to pay it comes from God.

Today we remember St Charles Borromeo, a rich young cardinal who counted the cost and gave everything for the reform of the Church and the care of the sick in time of plague. Tonight, let each of us ask: what comes before Christ in my life? Amen.
kids: Children, following Jesus is like building a tower: we plan, we pray and we never give up. Shine like little stars by being kind and honest!

homily: Dear friends, the Pharisees grumbled that Jesus welcomed sinners and ate with them. Jesus answered with two stories of searching: a shepherd who leaves ninety-nine sheep to find one, and a woman who lights a lamp and sweeps the whole house for one lost coin (Luke 15:4–8).

Notice who does the searching. It is not the sheep that finds the shepherd; it is the shepherd who finds the sheep. Before we ever looked for God, God was looking for us. And both stories end with a party: there is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents (Luke 15:7).

Paul shows us what it is like to be found. He had every reason for pride in his background and his zeal, yet he says that all of it is loss compared with knowing Christ Jesus his Lord (Philippians 3:7–8). When Christ finds us, our old treasures lose their shine.

Who is the one lost sheep in your family or your street? Someone who has stopped coming to church, someone who feels forgotten? This week, be the shepherd's hands: make the call, pay the visit, light the lamp. Heaven is waiting to rejoice. Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus is the good shepherd who looks for every lost sheep. If someone in your class is alone, go and find them. Heaven will be happy!

homily: Dear friends, today's parable surprises everyone. A dishonest manager is about to lose his job, so he quickly reduces the debts of his master's debtors to win friends for the future. And the master praises him (Luke 16:8). Jesus does not praise his dishonesty; he praises his shrewdness.

The point is a challenge. People of this world put great energy into their worldly plans: careers, houses, investments. Why are the children of light so slow and careless about eternal things? If we planned our souls the way we plan our savings, how different our lives would be.

Paul gives the reason for urgency: our citizenship is in heaven, and from there we expect a Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body (Philippians 3:20–21). We are citizens of another country, living here for a while.

This is the first Friday of the month, a day to honour the Heart of Jesus. Let us be shrewd for the Kingdom: one clear spiritual goal for this November, written down and kept where we can see it. Amen.
kids: Children, we plan our games and our holidays. Let us also plan to be close to Jesus: one prayer, one good deed, every day!

homily: Dear friends, Jesus draws the lesson from yesterday's parable: whoever is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much (Luke 16:10). Money is a very little compared with the true riches of the Kingdom, but the way we handle it shows what is in our heart.

Then he draws a sharp line: you cannot serve God and wealth (Luke 16:13). Wealth is not evil in itself, but it always wants to become a master. The Pharisees, lovers of money, laughed at him; Jesus answered that God knows their hearts.

Paul thanks the Philippians for their gifts and tells them his secret: he has learned to be content with little or with plenty, because he can do all things through him who strengthens him (Philippians 4:12–13). A free heart is not owned by its possessions.

Here is a practical step: decide on a regular share of your income for God and for the poor, and give it first, not from what is left over. It is a small thing, but faithfulness in small things is the training ground for great ones. Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus says that if we are honest in little things, we will be trusted with big things. Share something you have with someone who needs it today!

homily: Dear friends, Jesus tells a short parable that cuts against our habit of keeping score with God. A servant who has worked all day in the field does not expect his master to serve him supper. So we too, when we have done all we were told, should say: we are unworthy servants; we have only done our duty (Luke 17:10).

Unworthy here means owed nothing. We cannot put God in our debt. Every good thing we do is already his gift. This is not a humiliation but a freedom: we serve out of love, not to earn a wage, and so we are never disappointed.

Paul tells Titus why: the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to all, training us to live self-controlled, upright and godly lives while we wait for the blessed hope (Titus 2:11–13). Grace is not only a gift to receive but a teacher to follow.

Today we honour St Leo the Great, Pope, who defended the truth that Christ is true God and true man, and who faced Attila with nothing but prayer. Let us serve today without counting, and thank God for the privilege of serving at all. Amen.
kids: Children, we do good not to get a prize but because we love Jesus. Help at home today without being asked!

homily: Dear friends, ten lepers stood at a distance and cried out: Jesus, Master, have mercy on us. Jesus sent them to the priests, and on the way they were cleansed (Luke 17:12–14). All ten were healed. Only one came back, praising God with a loud voice and falling at Jesus' feet, and he was a Samaritan, a foreigner.

Jesus asks: were not ten made clean? Where are the other nine? And to the one who returned he says: your faith has made you well (Luke 17:17–19), or, as the word also means, has saved you. Ten received healing; one received salvation, because he came back to the Healer.

Paul reminds Titus that God saved us not because of any works of righteousness that we had done, but according to his mercy, through the water of rebirth and renewal by the Holy Spirit (Titus 3:5). Everything begins with mercy, and mercy received calls for thanks.

Today we remember St Martin of Tours, the soldier who shared his cloak with a beggar and saw Christ wearing it that night. Gratitude turned into generosity. Let us keep a list this week: three thanks each night, and one act of mercy each day. Amen.
kids: Children, only one leper said thank you to Jesus. Let us be like him! Tonight, tell Jesus three things you are thankful for.

homily: Dear friends, the Pharisees wanted signs and dates: when will the Kingdom come? Jesus answered that the Kingdom of God is not coming with things that can be observed; it is already among you (Luke 17:20–21). It is present in his own person.

And he adds a hard word: before the day of the Son of Man, he must endure much suffering and be rejected by this generation (Luke 17:25). The Kingdom does not come through power and spectacle; it comes through the Cross.

The short letter to Philemon shows the Kingdom at work in a household. Paul sends back a runaway slave, Onesimus, who has become a Christian, and asks Philemon to receive him no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother (Philemon 16). The Gospel quietly changes the most ordinary relationships.

Today we honour St Josaphat, who gave his life for the unity of Christians. The Kingdom is among us when walls come down: between master and servant, between Churches, between neighbours. Treat someone today who serves you as a brother or sister. Amen.
kids: Children, God's Kingdom is wherever people love one another like brothers and sisters. Be kind today to someone who helps you: a driver, a cleaner, a cook.

homily: Dear friends, Jesus compares the day of the Son of Man to the days of Noah and of Lot. People were eating and drinking, marrying, buying and selling, planting and building, until the flood came or fire fell (Luke 17:26–29). None of these things is wrong. Their sin was living as if God did not exist.

Then a strange command: remember Lot's wife (Luke 17:32). She was rescued from Sodom but looked back, longing for what she was leaving, and was lost. Whoever tries to keep his life will lose it, and whoever loses it will keep it.

St John, in his second letter, gives the simple rule for these days: walk in truth and in love, according to the commandment we have had from the beginning, that we love one another (2 John 4–6). Readiness is not anxiety; it is faithfulness in ordinary days.

So let us make a short examen each night this week before sleep: where was God today, where did I forget him, what will I do better tomorrow? Then the day of the Lord will find us looking forward, not back. Amen.
kids: Children, Noah was ready when the rain came because he listened to God. Before you sleep tonight, say: thank you, sorry, and please help me tomorrow.

homily: Dear friends, Luke tells us the point before the parable: we need to pray always and not to lose heart (Luke 18:1). A widow, the most powerless person in that society, keeps coming to an unjust judge until he gives her justice just to be rid of her.

If even such a judge gives in to persistence, how much more will God, who is not unjust but a loving Father, grant justice to his chosen ones who cry to him day and night (Luke 18:7)? God is not reluctant. But persistent prayer changes us: it keeps our hope alive and our hearts turned to him.

Then Jesus asks a haunting question: when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on earth (Luke 18:8)? Faith is not only believing once; it is continuing to pray when the answer is slow. St John, in his third letter, praises Gaius for supporting the missionaries and so becoming a co-worker with the truth (3 John 8).
Choose one intention today, for a person, a healing, a reconciliation, and pray for it every day until Advent begins. Do not lose heart. The Father hears. Amen.
kids: Children, the widow kept asking and never gave up. Choose one person to pray for every day this month, and keep going!

homily: Dear friends, in these last weeks of the year the Church reads the Book of Revelation. Today the risen Christ speaks to the church of Ephesus. He praises its hard work and endurance, but he has one complaint: you have abandoned the love you had at first (Revelation 2:4). A community can be correct and busy and still have grown cold.

The remedy is threefold: remember from where you have fallen, repent, and do the works you did at first (Revelation 2:5). Remember the joy of your First Communion, your wedding day, your first steps in prayer. Love is renewed by returning to its source.

Near Jericho a blind beggar hears that Jesus is passing by and cries out: Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me! The crowd tells him to be quiet, and he cries out all the more. Jesus asks: what do you want me to do for you? Lord, let me see again (Luke 18:38–41).

Let us make his prayer our own: Lord, let me see. Let me see where my love has cooled, and let me see you again as I saw you at first. And when we see, let us do what the blind man did: follow him, glorifying God. Amen.
kids: Children, the blind man shouted to Jesus and did not stop. Jesus heard him! Pray today: Jesus, help me to see you in everyone.

homily: Dear friends, to the church of Laodicea, rich and comfortable, Christ speaks his sharpest words: because you are lukewarm, neither cold nor hot, I am about to spit you out of my mouth (Revelation 3:16). Comfort can make a Christian lukewarm without his noticing.

But immediately follow the tenderest words in the book: I am standing at the door, knocking; if you hear my voice and open the door, I will come in and eat with you, and you with me (Revelation 3:20). Christ does not break doors. He knocks, and waits.

Zacchaeus, a chief tax collector and rich, wanted to see Jesus, and because he was short he climbed a sycamore tree. Jesus stopped, looked up and said: Zacchaeus, hurry down, for I must stay at your house today. And salvation came to that house as Zacchaeus gave half his goods to the poor (Luke 19:5–9).

Today we remember St Elizabeth of Hungary, a young princess who opened the door of her heart and her treasury to the poor. Where is Christ knocking in your life today? Open the door: one generous gift, one visit, one reconciliation. Amen.
kids: Children, Zacchaeus climbed a tree to see Jesus, and Jesus came to his house! Open your heart to Jesus today by sharing with someone in need.

homily: Dear friends, today John is taken up through an open door in heaven. He sees the throne of God, the four living creatures who sing day and night without ceasing: Holy, holy, holy, the Lord God the Almighty, who was and is and is to come, and the twenty-four elders casting their crowns before the throne (Revelation 4:8–10).

This is the worship that never stops, and every Mass joins it when we sing the Holy, holy, holy. At the altar we do not only remember heaven; we are united with it. All our work on earth finds its meaning before that throne.

In the Gospel a nobleman goes to a distant country to receive a kingdom and gives each servant a pound to trade with. To the one who made ten more he says: well done, good servant; because you have been trustworthy in a very small thing, take charge of ten cities (Luke 19:17). The fearful servant who hid his pound lost even that.

God has entrusted gifts to each of us: time, talents, faith. Let us not bury them out of fear. Offer your work to God each morning this week, and let your ordinary tasks become part of heaven's song. Amen.
kids: Children, in heaven the angels sing Holy, holy, holy. We sing it too at Mass! Use the gifts God gave you today: your voice, your hands, your smile.

homily: Dear friends, in heaven no one is found worthy to open the sealed scroll of history, and John weeps bitterly. Then he is told: the Lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered. He looks, and sees not a lion but a Lamb standing as if it had been slaughtered (Revelation 5:5–6).

This is the surprise at the heart of our faith. Christ's victory is not the victory of force but of self-giving love. The heavenly court sings a new song: by your blood you ransomed for God saints from every tribe and language and people and nation (Revelation 5:9). Kerala, Vietnam, Germany, Italy: all are in that song.

In the Gospel, Jesus comes near Jerusalem, sees the city and weeps over it: if you had only recognised on this day the things that make for peace (Luke 19:42). God does not watch our wars and divisions coldly. He weeps over them.
The Lamb conquers by love, and he calls us to be people of peace. Pray for peace in the world each day this week, and make peace in your own home: one apology, one kind word, one forgiven hurt. Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus is the Lamb of God who loves everyone in the world. He cried for his city because he wanted peace. Make peace with someone today!

homily: Dear friends, John is told to take the little scroll from the angel's hand and eat it. It was sweet as honey in his mouth, but when he had eaten it his stomach was made bitter (Revelation 10:9–10). Like Ezekiel before him, the prophet must first digest God's word before he can speak it.

The word is sweet because it is God's: it consoles, it heals, it gives hope. It is also bitter, because it calls us to conversion and carries the cost of the Cross. Whoever proclaims it, parent, catechist or priest, must first let it enter his own life.

In the Gospel Jesus enters the Temple and drives out those who were selling, saying: my house shall be a house of prayer, but you have made it a den of robbers. And every day he was teaching in the Temple, and all the people were spellbound by what they heard (Luke 19:46–48).

Our churches, our homes and our hearts are meant to be houses of prayer. Let us clear out what crowds God out, and let us eat his word: read the Sunday Gospel at home every Saturday evening, slowly, so that on Sunday it is already in us. Amen.
kids: Children, God's word is sweeter than honey! Ask your parents to read the Sunday Gospel with you on Saturday night.

homily: Dear friends, in this last week of the Church's year, Jesus sits near the Temple treasury and watches people putting in their gifts. The rich put in large sums; a poor widow puts in two small copper coins. Jesus says she has put in more than all of them, for they gave out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty gave all she had to live on (Luke 21:3–4).
God does not measure a gift by its size, but by the love and trust it carries. The widow trusted God with her whole living. That is why her two coins outweigh all the gold.

In Revelation John sees the Lamb standing on Mount Zion with those who bear his name and his Father's name on their foreheads; they follow the Lamb wherever he goes (Revelation 14:1, 4). The widow belongs to them: she follows the Lamb who will soon give not two coins but his whole life.
Let us ask ourselves honestly: do I give God what is left over, or do I give him my heart? Today, give something that truly costs you, in money, in time or in patience, and give it with joy. Amen.
kids: Children, the poor widow gave only two little coins, but Jesus said she gave the most, because she gave with all her heart. Give Jesus your best today!

homily: Dear friends, people were admiring the Temple with its beautiful stones and gifts. Jesus said: the days will come when not one stone will be left upon another (Luke 21:6). Even the holiest building on earth does not last for ever; only God's word remains.

Then he warns: beware that you are not led astray, for many will come in my name and say, the time is near. Do not go after them. When you hear of wars and insurrections, do not be terrified (Luke 21:8–9). Christian hope is calm, not alarmist. We do not need to chase predictions; we need to stay faithful.

Revelation pictures the end as a harvest: one like a Son of Man on a cloud swings his sickle, for the harvest of the earth is fully ripe (Revelation 14:15). The judgement belongs to God, and it comes in his time, not ours.

Today we honour St Andrew Dũng-Lạc and the martyrs of Vietnam: priests, catechists, fathers and mothers, who lived this calm hope under persecution. They were ripe wheat gathered into God's barn. Let us pray today for Christians who suffer for their faith, and let us share hope, not fear. Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus says: do not be afraid. The martyrs of Vietnam loved Jesus even when it was dangerous. Pray today for children who cannot go to church freely.

homily: Dear friends, Jesus does not promise his disciples an easy road. They will be arrested and persecuted, handed over to synagogues and prisons, brought before kings and governors, even betrayed by parents, brothers and friends. But he turns it around: this will give you an opportunity to testify (Luke 21:12–13).

He promises words and a wisdom that none of their opponents will be able to withstand, and then a paradox: some of you will be put to death, yet not a hair of your head will perish. By your endurance you will gain your souls (Luke 21:16–19). Our final security is not survival, but belonging to God.

Revelation shows where this endurance ends: the conquerors stand beside a sea of glass mixed with fire, holding harps, and sing the song of Moses and the song of the Lamb (Revelation 15:2–3). As Israel sang after crossing the sea, the faithful sing after the trial.

Today the Church remembers St Catherine of Alexandria, honoured by tradition as a young woman who defended the faith with wisdom. When your faith is mocked, at school, at work or online, answer calmly and kindly. And keep one good resolution you are tempted to drop. Endurance wins the soul. Amen.
kids: Children, being a friend of Jesus is not always easy, but Jesus promises to give us the right words. If someone laughs at your faith, stay kind and brave!

homily: Dear friends, Jesus speaks of Jerusalem surrounded by armies, fulfilled in the year 70, and then of signs in the sun, the moon and the stars, nations in distress, people fainting from fear. And in the middle of it all he gives an unexpected command: stand up and raise your heads, because your redemption is drawing near (Luke 21:28).

What makes others faint makes disciples look up. The coming of the Son of Man in power and great glory is not a threat to those who love him; it is their liberation. We are not people of fear but of hope.

Revelation tells the same story in two pictures. Babylon, the proud city of luxury, idolatry and oppression, falls: fallen, fallen is Babylon the great (Revelation 18:2). And a wedding is announced: blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9). Every empire built on pride ends in ruins; the Bride of the Lamb is invited to a feast.

At every Mass, before Communion, the priest echoes this invitation. Let us prepare for that supper with care this Sunday: a moment of silence before Mass, and, if we need it, a good confession before Advent begins. Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus says: when you hear bad news, look up, because I am near! Before Communion on Sunday, close your eyes and tell Jesus you are happy he is coming.

homily: Dear friends, Jesus points to the fig tree: as soon as it sprouts leaves, you know that summer is near. So also, when you see these things taking place, you know that the kingdom of God is near (Luke 21:29–31). The events of history are signs that God's Kingdom is on its way.

Then he says a sentence of astonishing authority: heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away (Luke 21:33). Only God can say that. Mountains, empires, even the stars will fade; the Word made flesh will not.

Revelation shows the last judgement: the dead, great and small, standing before the throne, and the books opened, including the book of life (Revelation 20:12). And then the vision of hope: a new heaven and a new earth, and the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband (Revelation 21:1–2). God does not throw creation away; he makes it new.

Let us build our lives on what does not pass away. Write one verse of the Gospel on a card and carry it with you this week. And look around you today for one sign that God's Kingdom is growing: a kindness, a reconciliation, a prayer answered. Amen.
kids: Children, flowers and trees fade, but Jesus' words last for ever. Learn one verse of the Bible by heart this week!

homily: Dear friends, the Church's year ends today with the last page of the Bible. The angel shows John the river of the water of life, bright as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb, and the tree of life whose leaves are for the healing of the nations (Revelation 22:1–2). The tree lost in Eden is given back.

There will be no more night; they need no light of lamp or sun, for the Lord God will be their light (Revelation 22:5). And the last promise: see, I am coming soon (Revelation 22:7). The whole of history moves toward that light.

Jesus' last words in Luke's discourse are practical: be on guard so that your hearts are not weighed down with dissipation and drunkenness and the worries of this life. Be alert at all times, praying (Luke 21:34–36). These are perfect words for the threshold of Advent.

This evening, with First Vespers, the Church begins a new year, praying the prayer of the first Christians: Marana tha, Come, Lord Jesus. Prepare an Advent wreath for your home today, and choose one Advent fast to lighten your heart. Amen.
kids: Children, tomorrow Advent begins! Help your family prepare an Advent wreath and light the first candle together, saying: Come, Lord Jesus!

intro: Theme: “A multitude no one could count.”
All Saints: the Church in glory shows the Church on earth her destiny and the way to it, the Beatitudes.

sub: Holiness is God's own life shared with us.
The call is for every baptised person, not a few.
The saints are our family, not distant heroes.
q: Speak to all the congregation of the people of Israel and say to them: You shall be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy.

After this I looked, and there was a great multitude that no one could count, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb, robed in white, with palm branches in their hands.
points.apply: Thank God for the holy people in your own family.

points.h: Washed in the blood of the Lamb
sub: The white robes are not self-made.
Every saint is a forgiven sinner.
Confession keeps the baptismal robe white.
q: Who shall ascend the hill of the LORD? And who shall stand in his holy place? Those who have clean hands and pure hearts, who do not lift up their souls to what is false, and do not swear deceitfully.
