An echo of Isaiah 45:23, where God says, “To me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall swear.” What Isaiah says of the Lord, Paul says of Jesus: “Lord” (kyrios) is the name of God.
ch: The Catechism quotes this hymn when it teaches the Incarnation (CCC 461) and when it explains that the first confessions of faith gave Jesus the divine title “Lord” (CCC 449). The Church has always held that in emptying himself the Son remained fully God while becoming fully man: this is the faith of the Council of Chalcedon (451). The hymn is sung every Saturday evening in Evening Prayer of the Liturgy of the Hours.

r.h: Come, for everything is ready now
set: Jesus is at a Sabbath dinner in the house of a leader of the Pharisees (14:1). He has just told his host to invite “the poor, the crippled, the lame, and the blind” (14:13). A guest responds with a pious remark about the banquet of the kingdom, and Jesus answers with a parable. In that culture an important host sent a first invitation and then, when the meal was ready, a servant to call the guests.
str: v. 15: “Blessed is anyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God!”
vv. 16–17: the invitation and the call.
vv. 18–20: three excuses: land, oxen, marriage.
vv. 21–23: the poor and the disabled of the town, then those on the roads outside.
v. 24: none of the first guests will taste the dinner.
kw: The banquet is a common biblical image of the kingdom (Isaiah 25:6).
Literally “to ask to be let off”. The excuses are polite, and each concerns a good thing. But each puts something else before the host.
Not force but urgent, insistent hospitality: in the East a humble person would refuse an invitation at first and had to be pressed to come.
vv: ‘Come; for everything is ready now.’
The time of the kingdom has come in Jesus. Nothing remains to be prepared except the guests’ answer.
‘Go out at once into the streets and lanes of the town and bring in the poor, the crippled, the blind, and the lame.’
The same four groups as in 14:13. The host does what Jesus has just asked the Pharisee to do.
and compel people to come in, so that my house may be filled.
The host wants a full house. Luke’s readers saw here the mission to the nations beyond Israel.
ch: Before Communion the priest says, “Blessed are those called to the supper of the Lamb” (compare Revelation 19:9). Every Mass is this invitation. St Augustine once used “compel them to come in” to justify pressure on the Donatists; the Church today teaches clearly that no one may be forced to embrace the faith (Dignitatis Humanae 10). The compulsion of the parable is the urgency of love.

qa: Did Christ stop being God when he “emptied himself”?
No. He took on what he was not, our human nature, without losing what he was. He “humbled himself”: the emptying was a choice of love, not a loss of divinity (CCC 464, 469).
study: Philippians 2:5 asks us to have the mind of Christ. In which relationship do I most need his humility?
Which good thing (my “field”, my “oxen”) most often becomes my excuse not to come to the Lord’s table?

lead: Paul tells the Philippians to work out their salvation, knowing that God is at work in them, and to shine like stars. Jesus tells the crowds that following him means carrying the cross and counting the cost. Today the Church remembers St Charles Borromeo, a bishop who did both.

r.h: Shine like stars in the world
set: Right after the hymn of Christ’s self-emptying, Paul draws the practical lesson with “Therefore”. The Philippians must live out their salvation in a hostile city, without grumbling, while Paul himself may soon die in prison.
str: vv. 12–13: work out your salvation, for God is at work in you.
vv. 14–16: no murmuring; shine like stars, holding fast to the word of life.
vv. 17–18: even if Paul is poured out as a libation, he rejoices, and they must rejoice with him.
kw: To bring to completion what has been given. Salvation is God’s gift, but it must be lived.
The word for the heavenly lights in Genesis 1:14 (Greek). Compare Daniel 12:3: the wise “shall shine like the brightness of the sky”.
I am poured out as a libation
A drink offering poured over a sacrifice. Paul sees his possible death as an offering added to the Philippians’ sacrifice of faith.
vv: work out your own salvation with fear and trembling; for it is God who is at work in you, enabling you both to will and to work for his good pleasure.
The two halves belong together. We work because God works; our effort is the fruit of his grace, not a rival to it. “Fear and trembling” is reverence before God at work, not anxiety.
children of God without blemish in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation, in which you shine like stars in the world.
Paul takes the words of Deuteronomy 32:5, where a “crooked and perverse generation” described unfaithful Israel, and gives the believers the opposite calling: to be blameless children of God.
ch: St Augustine often quoted Philippians 2:13 to teach that God works in us both the willing and the doing, so that our good works are at the same time his gifts and truly ours (in substance). The Church teaches that grace does not take away our freedom but heals and raises it: the grace of Christ is not a rival of our freedom (CCC 1742).

r.h: Count the cost
set: Large crowds are now walking with Jesus toward Jerusalem, where the cross awaits him (9:51). He turns to them and tells them plainly what being his disciple will cost.
str: vv. 25–27: two conditions: to “hate” family and life, and to carry the cross.
vv. 28–32: two parables: the tower builder and the king going to war.
v. 33: the conclusion: renounce all possessions.
kw: A Semitic way of saying “love less, put second” (compare Genesis 29:30–31, where Leah is “unloved”, that is, loved less than Rachel). Matthew’s parallel says: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me” (Matthew 10:37).
For Luke’s readers, carrying the cross meant the walk of a condemned man to execution. Luke adds “daily” in 9:23.
To say farewell to, to take leave of. The disciple loosens his grip on everything he owns.
vv: Whoever does not carry the cross and follow me cannot be my disciple.
For which of you, intending to build a tower, does not first sit down and estimate the cost, to see whether he has enough to complete it?
Jesus does not want enthusiasm that dies halfway. Discipleship is a decision made with open eyes.
So therefore, none of you can become my disciple if you do not give up all your possessions.
ch: The Catechism quotes this verse: Jesus enjoins his disciples to prefer him to everything and everyone and to renounce all that they have for his sake (CCC 2544). This detachment takes different forms in religious, priests and lay people, but it is asked of all: nothing may come before Christ.

qa: Does Jesus really want us to hate our parents?
No. He commands us to honour them (Luke 18:20). “Hate” here is a Semitic idiom for choosing one thing over another. When love for family and love for Christ conflict, Christ must come first.
rite: St Charles Borromeo (1538–1584), Archbishop of Milan, was a nephew of Pope Pius IV and helped bring the Council of Trent to its conclusion. He worked on the Roman Catechism, founded seminaries for the training of priests, visited every parish of his huge diocese, and stayed with his people during the plague of 1576, caring for the sick and selling his goods for the poor. His motto was Humilitas, humility. He shows what today’s readings ask: a life poured out, and the cost counted and paid.
study: Philippians 2:13 says God is at work in me. Where do I see his work in my will and actions this week?
Which “tower” in my life have I begun without counting the cost, and what would it take to finish it with Christ?

lead: Paul counts all his gains as loss for the surpassing value of knowing Christ. In the Gospel the shepherd and the woman count their losses differently: one lost sheep and one lost coin are worth a search and a party. Both readings are about what is truly precious.

r.h: I regard everything as loss
set: In chapter 3 Paul warns the Philippians against Christian teachers who insisted that Gentile believers must be circumcised and keep the Law of Moses in order to belong fully to God’s people. Paul answers by telling his own story. He is not attacking Judaism or the Jewish people, whose gifts he honours (Romans 9:4–5); he is saying that nothing can be added to Christ.
str: v. 3: who the true circumcision is: those who worship in the Spirit and boast in Christ.
vv. 4–6: Paul’s own credentials.
vv. 7–8a: the great revaluation: gain becomes loss.
kw: Words from bookkeeping. Paul rewrites his account: what was in the profit column now stands under loss.
Not only knowledge about Christ but a personal knowledge, as of a friend. Paul goes on: “I want to know Christ and the power of his resurrection” (3:10).
A strong, blunt word: refuse, dung. Compared with Christ, even good things lose all value as a ground of boasting.
vv: circumcised on the eighth day, a member of the people of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew born of Hebrews; as to the law, a Pharisee;
Paul is proud of his people. Benjamin gave Israel its first king, Saul, whose name Paul bore.
Yet whatever gains I had, these I have come to regard as loss because of Christ.
More than that, I regard everything as loss because of the surpassing value of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord.
ch: The Catechism quotes this passage when it speaks of catechesis: whoever is called to teach Christ must first seek “the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus” (CCC 428). The heart of the Christian life is not a list of achievements but a person known and loved.

r.h: The lost sheep and the lost coin
set: Luke 15 is often called the heart of Luke’s Gospel. Tax collectors and sinners come to listen to Jesus; Pharisees and scribes grumble that he eats with them. Jesus answers with three parables of the lost: the sheep, the coin and the son (today’s reading gives the first two).
str: vv. 1–3: the setting: sinners come near; others grumble.
vv. 4–7: the shepherd and the lost sheep.
vv. 8–10: the woman and the lost coin.
¶ Each parable ends with a call to share joy: “Rejoice with me.”
kw: The word recalls Israel’s grumbling in the wilderness (Exodus 16:2, Greek). The complaint is that Jesus “welcomes” sinners and shares a table with them.
The same word as in 19:10: “the Son of Man came to seek out and to save the lost.”
A Greek silver coin, about a day’s wage. For a poor household, one coin in ten was a real loss.
vv: “This fellow welcomes sinners and eats with them.”
Meant as an accusation, it is a perfect summary of the Gospel.
When he has found it, he lays it on his shoulders and rejoices.
There is no scolding of the sheep. The shepherd carries it home himself.
Just so, I tell you, there is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner who repents.
“In the presence of the angels” is a reverent way of speaking of God himself. God rejoices.
ch: The Catechism says that the Gospel is the revelation in Jesus Christ of God’s mercy to sinners, and points to these parables (CCC 1846). St Gregory the Great saw in the woman who lights a lamp an image of the Wisdom of God, who lit the lamp of Christ’s humanity to seek the lost (in substance). Pope Francis, in Misericordiae Vultus 9, calls these the parables of mercy.

study: What “gains” do I still hold on to as reasons for confidence before God?
Whom do I find it hard to welcome to the table, and how would the shepherd of Luke 15 treat that person?

lead: Paul reminds the Philippians that their true citizenship is in heaven. Jesus tells a strange parable about a dishonest manager who is praised for his shrewdness. Both readings ask where we are really heading and how wisely we use the time we have.

r.h: Our citizenship is in heaven
set: Philippi was a Roman colony. Many of its people were proud to be citizens of Rome, enrolled in the far-off capital and living by its laws. Paul uses this pride to describe Christians: their true city is heaven, and they live here as its citizens. He contrasts them with people who live “as enemies of the cross”; who they were is debated, but they seem to have been self-indulgent believers who avoided the way of suffering.
str: v. 17: imitate me and those who live by our example.
vv. 18–19: the enemies of the cross, described with tears.
vv. 20–21: our citizenship and our hope: the Lord will transform our bodies.
4:1: stand firm in the Lord.
kw: The community of citizens and the rights it gives. Christians belong to the heavenly city before any earthly one.
A title often given to emperors. Paul gives it to Jesus Christ alone.
The same root as “form” (morphē) in the hymn of 2:6–7. The one who took the form of a slave will give us the form of his glory.
vv: For many live as enemies of the cross of Christ; I have often told you of them, and now I tell you even with tears.
Paul weeps over them; he does not mock them.
But our citizenship is in heaven, and it is from there that we are expecting a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ.
He will transform the body of our humiliation that it may be conformed to the body of his glory
Christian hope is not an escape from the body but its transformation. This verse is a basis for the Church’s faith in the resurrection of the body.
ch: The ancient Letter to Diognetus says that Christians live in their own countries as sojourners; they pass their days on earth, but they are citizens of heaven (in substance, ch. 5). The Church teaches that this hope does not make us careless about the earthly city but gives us a stronger reason to serve it (Gaudium et Spes 39).

r.h: The shrewd manager
set: Luke 16 is about the use of wealth. A rich man’s manager, an agent with authority over his master’s accounts, is accused of wasting the property and is about to be dismissed. He quickly reduces the debts of his master’s debtors so that they will receive him into their homes later.
str: vv. 1–2: the charge and the dismissal.
vv. 3–4: the manager’s reflection.
vv. 5–7: the debts reduced.
v. 8: the master praises his shrewdness; the lesson about the children of this age and the children of light.
kw: The word gives us “economy”. Every disciple is a steward, not an owner, of what he has.
Prudently, with practical wisdom. The master praises the manager’s quick and decisive thinking, not his dishonesty.
A phrase also found in the Dead Sea Scrolls for the faithful community. Jesus wishes they were as alert about the kingdom as worldly people are about money.
vv: I am not strong enough to dig, and I am ashamed to beg.
The manager faces his future honestly and acts at once. That is the point of comparison.
And his master commended the dishonest manager because he had acted shrewdly; for the children of this age are more shrewd in dealing with their own generation than are the children of light.

Some scholars think the manager removed his own commission or a hidden interest from the bills, so that he was sacrificing his own gain. Either way, the parable does not praise the cheating but the decisiveness in a crisis.
ch: The Catechism calls prudence “the charioteer of the virtues”, the virtue that disposes us to see our true good in every circumstance and to choose the right means to reach it (CCC 1806). The parable asks Christians to bring to the kingdom the energy and intelligence others bring to their business.

qa: Does Jesus praise dishonesty?

No. The master (and Jesus) praise the manager’s shrewdness, not his fraud; he is still called “the dishonest manager”. Jesus often uses unlikely figures to make a point, like the unjust judge in 18:1–8.
study: If my true citizenship is in heaven, what “laws” of that city should shape my choices this week?
Where do I show more energy for worldly matters than for the things of God?

lead: Paul thanks the Philippians for their gift and says he has learned to be content in every circumstance, because he can do all things in Christ. Jesus teaches that we cannot serve both God and wealth. Money is a test of where the heart rests.

r.h: I can do all things through him who strengthens me
set: At the end of the letter Paul thanks the Philippians for a gift they sent him in prison through Epaphroditus (2:25; 4:18). They had helped him from the beginning, even when he was in Thessalonica. Paul wants to thank them without suggesting that his peace depended on their money.
str: v. 10: joy at their renewed care.
vv. 11–13: the secret of contentment.
vv. 14–17: their past sharing and its true profit.
vv. 18–19: the gift as a sacrifice; God will supply every need.
kw: A word of the Stoic philosophers for self-sufficiency. Paul changes its meaning: his sufficiency is not in himself but in Christ (v. 13).
Literally “I have been initiated”, a word used of the mystery religions. Paul’s secret is learned through experience with Christ.
The language of Old Testament sacrifice (Genesis 8:21; Exodus 29:18). A gift to a poor apostle is worship offered to God.
vv: Not that I am referring to being in need; for I have learned to be content with whatever I have.
I can do all things through him who strengthens me.
In its context, this verse is about contentment in hunger and plenty. “All things” means facing every situation, rich or poor, with Christ’s strength.
And my God will fully satisfy every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus.
They supplied Paul’s need; God will supply theirs. Generosity does not empty us.
ch: Paul calls a gift of money “a sacrifice acceptable and pleasing to God”. The Catechism notes that from the very beginning Christians have brought, with the bread and wine for the Eucharist, gifts to share with those in need (CCC 1351). The collection at Mass belongs to this tradition.

r.h: You cannot serve God and wealth
set: These sayings follow the parable of the shrewd manager and draw lessons from it about the use of money. Luke notes that some Pharisees who heard this “were lovers of money” and laughed at Jesus. Luke speaks of these particular listeners, not of the Pharisees as a whole.
str: v. 9: make friends by means of dishonest wealth.
vv. 10–12: faithfulness in little and in much.
v. 13: no one can serve two masters.
vv. 14–15: the response of the listeners and Jesus’ answer.
kw: An Aramaic word for property or money, perhaps from a root meaning that in which one trusts. Jesus treats it as a rival master.
Literally “eternal tents”, the dwellings of the age to come.
A strong word, used in the Old Testament for idolatry. What people prize above God becomes an idol.
vv: make friends for yourselves by means of dishonest wealth so that when it is gone, they may welcome you into the eternal homes.
Money will fail us at death. Used for the poor, it makes friends who will welcome us. “Dishonest wealth” means worldly money, which so easily leads to injustice.
Whoever is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much;
No slave can serve two masters;
Jesus does not say “should not” but “cannot”. Money is a servant, never a master.
ch: The Catechism counts the service of money among the forms of idolatry, and cites the Lord’s word, “You cannot serve God and mammon” (CCC 2113). It also quotes St John Chrysostom: not to enable the poor to share in our goods is to steal from them and deprive them of life (CCC 2446).

study: Paul learned contentment “in any and all circumstances”. What do I find it hardest to be content without?
Who are the “friends” my money is making for eternity?

lead: The Church is near the end of her year. In November she prays for the dead, and the Sunday readings turn to the last things: death, the coming of the Lord, and how to be ready. Today the Lectionary pairs a poem about Wisdom with the parable of the wise and foolish bridesmaids, and the link is in the word itself. Wisdom “is found by those who seek her” and waits “at the gate”; the wise bridesmaids are those who are ready when the door opens.

The psalm gives the voice of the seeker: “my soul thirsts for you”, a prayer of the night and of the dawn. St Paul, writing to a young Church that was grieving its first dead, tells them that those who have died in Christ are not lost: the Lord will come, and “so we will be with the Lord forever”. Seeking, thirsting, hoping and keeping awake: these are the four movements of the day.

r.h: Wisdom waits at the door
set: The Book of Wisdom was written in Greek, most likely at Alexandria in Egypt, in the century before Christ. Its author is a devout Jewish teacher who speaks in the person of Solomon, the wise king, to encourage faithful Jews living among Greek culture. It belongs to the deuterocanonical books, received by the Catholic Church as inspired Scripture.

Chapter 6 is a hinge. Chapters 1–5 speak of the destiny of the just and the wicked; from chapter 6 the book turns to praise Wisdom herself. The chapter opens with an address to kings and judges (6:1): those who rule others must first seek Wisdom. Our passage is the invitation that follows.
str: v. 12: Wisdom is radiant and does not fade; those who love and seek her find her.
v. 13: she hurries to make herself known.
v. 14: whoever rises early to seek her finds her already sitting at the gate.
v. 15: to think of her is understanding; to keep watch for her brings relief from anxiety.
v. 16: she goes about seeking those worthy of her.
¶ The passage moves in a circle. It begins with us seeking Wisdom (v. 12) and ends with Wisdom seeking us (v. 16). The search is real, but the one we seek is already looking for us.
kw: In this book Wisdom is spoken of as a person, a radiant woman who comes from God (see 7:25–26). She is not a goddess; she is God’s own wisdom reaching out to human beings.
The verb used in v. 14 means to get up at dawn for a purpose. The Greek of Psalm 63, today’s psalm, uses the same verb: “to you I rise at dawn”. Seeking God is a morning work.
to keep watch, to stay awake
Used in v. 15 for the one who is vigilant on Wisdom’s account. It is the attitude the Gospel asks of the bridesmaids: “Keep awake”.
vv: Wisdom is radiant and unfading, and she is easily discerned by those who love her, and is found by those who seek her.
Love comes before seeing. Wisdom is not first a matter of cleverness but of desire: those who love her recognise her.
One who rises early to seek her will have no difficulty, for she will be found sitting at the gate.

The gate of an ancient town was the place of business, judgment and meeting. The Greek speaks of the seeker’s own gates: the one who gets up early to look for Wisdom finds her already waiting at his door.
because she goes about seeking those worthy of her, and she graciously appears to them in their paths, and meets them in every thought.
Here the search is reversed. Wisdom walks the roads looking for people. This prepares the Christian reader for the Gospel, where the Son goes out to seek the lost.
ch: St Paul calls Christ “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24), and the Fathers read the great Wisdom poems as speaking of the eternal Son, the Word through whom all things were made (in substance). The Latin Church sings to him on 17 December, in the first of the O Antiphons: “O Wisdom, who came from the mouth of the Most High”. To seek Wisdom, for a Christian, is to seek Christ, and to discover that he has been seeking us first.

r.h: A thirst that keeps watch
set: The heading of the psalm places it in the wilderness of Judah, the dry hill country that falls away towards the Dead Sea, where David hid from his enemies. It is the prayer of someone far from the sanctuary who remembers having seen God there, and who longs for him as dry ground longs for rain.
str: vv. 2–4: longing, and the memory of God’s glory in the sanctuary.
vv. 5–6: praise and a soul satisfied as with a feast.
vv. 7–8: remembering God through the night, under the shadow of his wings.
kw: The word first means the throat, then the breath and the whole living self. When the psalmist says “my soul thirsts”, the thirst is felt in the whole person.
God’s faithful, covenant love. The psalm says this love is “better than life”: to be loved by God matters more than to be alive.
An image of shelter, like a bird covering its young, and perhaps also of the wings of the cherubim over the ark in the sanctuary.
vv: O God, you are my God, I seek you, my soul thirsts for you
The Greek and Latin versions read “to you I keep watch at dawn”, which is why this psalm has long been a morning prayer.
Because your steadfast love is better than life, my lips will praise you.
when I think of you on my bed, and meditate on you in the watches of the night
The night watches recall the midnight of the Gospel. The one who thinks of God in the night is the one who is awake when the cry comes.
ch: From early centuries the Church has sung this psalm at dawn, and the Liturgy of the Hours still gives it to Morning Prayer of the first Sunday of the four week cycle. On this Sunday it becomes the prayer of the wise bridesmaids: a soul that thirsts for God and keeps watch in the night.

r.h: We will be with the Lord forever
set: This is probably the oldest writing in the New Testament, from about AD 50–51. Paul had founded the Church at Thessalonica in northern Greece but had to leave in a hurry (Acts 17:1–10). The new Christians were waiting eagerly for the Lord’s return. When some of them died, the others were troubled: would the dead miss the coming of Christ?
Paul answers with the heart of the faith: Jesus died and rose, and those who belong to him share his destiny.
str: v. 13: the purpose: that you may not grieve like those who have no hope.
v. 14: the creed: Jesus died and rose again; so God will bring the dead with him.
vv. 15–17: a word of the Lord: the dead in Christ will rise first, and the living will join them to meet the Lord.
v. 18: therefore, encourage one another.
kw: The Greek word for those who have died, which the NRSV translates “those who have died” and the POC “those who have fallen asleep”. From the same root comes koimētērion, a sleeping place, our word “cemetery”. For Christians the grave is a bed, not an end.
The word used for the visit of an emperor or a governor to a city. Christians used it for the glorious coming of Christ.

When an important visitor came, the citizens went out of the city to meet him and escort him back in. Paul pictures the Church going out to meet her Lord. Matthew uses the same word in today’s Gospel: “Come out to meet him” (25:6).
vv: But we do not want you to be uninformed, brothers and sisters, about those who have died, so that you may not grieve as others do who have no hope.
Paul does not forbid grief. He forbids hopeless grief. Christians weep at a funeral, but they weep as people who expect to meet again.
For since we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so, through Jesus, God will bring with him those who have died.

The Greek can be read in two ways: “God will bring through Jesus those who have died”, or “God will bring with him those who have died through (that is, in) Jesus”. The POC takes the second way and speaks of those who have fallen asleep in Jesus. Both say the same thing: the dead are held by Christ.
Then we who are alive, who are left, will be caught up in the clouds together with them to meet the Lord in the air; and so we will be with the Lord forever.

The images are drawn from Old Testament pictures of God’s coming, clouds and trumpet (Exodus 19:16; Daniel 7:13). Paul does not give a timetable. His last words are the point: “we will be with the Lord forever”.
ch: The Catechism teaches that we will rise “on the last day”, citing this passage (CCC 1001), and that to live in heaven is “to be with Christ” (CCC 1025). The Roman Missal puts the same hope into the Preface for the Dead: for the faithful, life is changed, not ended (in substance). In November, when the Church prays for the faithful departed, Paul’s last line is her instruction to every family in mourning: “encourage one another with these words”.

r.h: The cry at midnight
set: Jesus speaks these words in Jerusalem, a few days before his Passion, on the Mount of Olives (24:3). His long teaching about the end (chapters 24–25) closes with three parables. This first one asks one question: who will be ready when the Lord comes, even if he comes late?

In village weddings of the time, the bridegroom came at night to bring his bride to his own house, and young women of the family went out with lights to welcome the procession and enter the feast with it. A delay was nothing unusual at such weddings.
str: vv. 1–4: ten young women, all with lamps; five also take oil.
vv. 5–7: the delay, the sleep, the cry at midnight, the lamps trimmed.
vv. 8–9: the request for oil and the refusal.
vv. 10–12: the door shut, the late knocking, “I do not know you”.
v. 13: the lesson for the listener.
kw: Probably a torch with a head of cloth soaked in oil, which burned for a short time and had to be fed. The foolish had lit their torches; what they lacked was the oil to keep them burning.
Oil in Scripture is a sign of joy, healing and anointing. In the parable it is the one thing the foolish cannot borrow.
A present imperative: keep on watching. It is the word Jesus will say to Peter, James and John in Gethsemane a few days later (26:38–41).
vv: But at midnight there was a shout, ‘Look! Here is the bridegroom! Come out to meet him.’
The arrival comes at the darkest hour, when no one expects it. The cry is good news: the one they were waiting for is here.
The foolish said to the wise, ‘Give us some of your oil, for our lamps are going out.’
The Greek is present tense: the lamps are going out. They had started well. What fails is not the beginning but the perseverance.
Keep awake therefore, for you know neither the day nor the hour.
All ten slept, so “keep awake” cannot mean never sleeping. It means living each day so that, whenever the call comes, the oil is there.
ch: St Augustine, preaching on this parable, saw the oil as charity, the love that keeps faith alive (in substance); St John Chrysostom saw it as mercy to the poor (in substance). Both point to a life of love that cannot be produced at the last moment. The Catechism reminds us that the Church is the bride who waits for the bridegroom (CCC 796), and that we must watch, since we know neither the day nor the hour (CCC 1036).

qa: Is 1 Thessalonians 4:17 about a secret “rapture” before the end?

The word “caught up” (Latin rapiemur) gave English the word “rapture”, but Paul is not describing a secret removal of believers. He is describing the one glorious coming of Christ, when the dead rise and the living join them to meet the Lord, as citizens go out to meet a king. The Catholic Church teaches one coming of Christ in glory at the end of time, followed by the resurrection and the judgment (CCC 1001, 1038–1040).
Were the wise bridesmaids selfish?

The parable is not a lesson in sharing goods; elsewhere Jesus commands generosity. It teaches that readiness for God is personal. Faith and love can be supported by others, but at the decisive moment no one can stand in for us.
Is the Book of Wisdom really part of the Bible?

Yes. Wisdom is one of the deuterocanonical books, part of the Greek Old Testament used by the early Church and received as Scripture by the Catholic Church (Council of Trent; CCC 120). The New Testament echoes it in several places.
rite: In the Roman calendar these are the last Sundays of the year. Next Sunday the readings speak of the talents, and on 22 November the year ends with Christ the King; Advent begins on 29 November. November is the month of the faithful departed, and many parishes read out the names of those who died in the past year. Today’s second reading is one of the readings the Lectionary offers for funerals. At every baptism a lighted candle is given with the prayer that the flame of faith be kept alive, so that when the Lord comes the newly baptised may go out to meet him with all the saints (in substance). Every baptised Catholic is one of the ten, holding a lamp.
study: Wisdom 6 begins with us seeking and ends with Wisdom seeking us. Where have I noticed God looking for me first?
Psalm 63 is a prayer of the night and the dawn. When in my day do I “thirst” for God?
How does 1 Thessalonians 4:13–18 change the way I grieve and pray for my own dead this November?
What is the “oil” that keeps my lamp burning, and what makes it run low?

lead: Today the whole Latin Church keeps the anniversary of the dedication of a church in Rome: the Basilica of St John Lateran, the cathedral of the Pope as Bishop of Rome. An inscription on its front calls it the mother and head of all the churches of the city and of the world. Yet the readings are not about stones. They move from a building to a living people and to the body of Christ.

Ezekiel sees a river flowing out of the Temple and bringing life wherever it goes. The psalm sings of a river that gladdens the city of God, because God is in her midst. Paul tells the Corinthians that they themselves are God’s temple, built on the one foundation, Jesus Christ. In John, Jesus cleanses the Temple and speaks of the temple of his body, destroyed and raised in three days. The line runs from the Temple to the Christ, and from the Christ to the Church: water, foundation and body.

r.h: The river from the sanctuary
set: Ezekiel was a priest taken to Babylon with the first exiles in 597 BC. He saw Jerusalem and its Temple destroyed in 587 BC. In the last part of his book (chapters 40–48), dated to the twenty-fifth year of the exile (40:1), he is shown in vision a new Temple, a renewed land and a renewed people. In chapter 43 the glory of the Lord returns to the Temple by the east gate. Now, from the same Temple, water begins to flow.
The river runs east, down through the desert of Judah to the Arabah and the Dead Sea, the lowest and saltiest water on earth, where nothing lives. This is the place the vision chooses to heal.
str: vv. 1–2: water comes out from under the threshold of the Temple, on the south side of the altar, and flows east.
vv. 3–7 (not read): measured every thousand cubits, the stream grows from ankle-deep to a river no one can cross.
vv. 8–9: the river reaches the Dead Sea and makes its water fresh; wherever it goes, everything lives.
v. 12: fruit trees on both banks, fruit every month and leaves for healing, because the water comes from the sanctuary.
kw: Usually a wadi, a valley that runs with water only after rain. Here it is a stream that grows deeper the farther it goes from its source, the opposite of every river in the desert.
The word for life returns again and again in v. 9: every creature “will live”, and “everything will live where the river goes”.
The leaves of the trees are “for healing”. The vision is not only of plenty but of a cure for what was wounded.
vv: there, water was flowing from below the threshold of the temple toward the east

The Hebrew word for south here also means “right”. The ancient Latin version reads “from the right side” of the Temple, and the Church’s Easter antiphon takes up these words: “I saw water flowing from the right side of the temple”.
Wherever the river goes, every living creature that swarms will live, and there will be very many fish, once these waters reach there.
The Dead Sea is named here only as “the sea of stagnant waters” (v. 8). The vision promises fish where there were none. Verse 10 even pictures fishermen spreading their nets along its shore.
Their fruit will be for food, and their leaves for healing.
ch: Jesus takes up this image in John 7:37–39: “out of the believer’s heart shall flow rivers of living water”, and John explains that he meant the Spirit. At the Cross, from the pierced side of Christ, “blood and water” flow out (John 19:34), and the Fathers saw there the birth of the Church and her sacraments of Baptism and the Eucharist (in substance). The Book of Revelation closes with the same river and trees whose leaves are “for the healing of the nations” (Revelation 22:1–2). In the Easter season the Roman rite sings the antiphon “Vidi aquam” as the people are sprinkled with water: the Temple from which the water flows is the risen Christ.

r.h: God is in the midst of the city
set: Psalm 46 is one of the Songs of Zion, which praise Jerusalem as the city where God dwells. It pictures the world shaking, mountains falling into the sea and nations in uproar, and in the middle of it all a city that does not move.
str: vv. 2–3: God our refuge, even if the earth changes and the mountains shake.
vv. 5–6: the river that gladdens the city; God in her midst.
vv. 8–9: the refrain, and an invitation to see the works of the Lord.
kw: A place of shelter from storm or attack. The psalm says that God himself, not walls, is the city’s refuge.
Jerusalem had no great river, only the spring of Gihon. The river of the psalm is God’s presence, which waters the city as a river waters a garden.
“The Lord of hosts is with us” uses the same words as the name Immanuel, “God is with us” (Isaiah 7:14; Matthew 1:23).
vv: God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.
There is a river whose streams make glad the city of God, the holy habitation of the Most High.
On this feast the psalm answers the first reading: the river of Ezekiel and the river of the psalm are one water, flowing from God’s dwelling.
The Lord of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our refuge.
ch: The Church applies the Songs of Zion to herself, the city of God built on the apostles, and above all to the presence of Christ in her midst. In every church that is dedicated, the psalm’s promise is made concrete: “God is in the midst of the city; it shall not be moved”.

r.h: You are God’s temple
set: The Church at Corinth was gifted and divided. Some said “I belong to Paul”, others “I belong to Apollos” or “to Cephas” (1:12). In chapter 3 Paul answers that all preachers are servants. The Church does not belong to them; it belongs to God. He uses two pictures: a field that God makes grow, and a building that God builds.
str: v. 9c: you are God’s building.
v. 10: Paul laid the foundation as a skilled master builder; others build on it with care.
v. 11: the only foundation is Jesus Christ.
vv. 12–15 (not read): the work of each builder will be tested by fire on the Day.
vv. 16–17: you are God’s temple; the Spirit of God dwells in you; God’s temple is holy.
kw: Both the building and the act of building. The Church is never finished; it is always under construction.
The chief builder who lays out the foundation. Paul does not boast of it: he did it “according to the grace of God given to me”.
Not the whole Temple precinct but the sanctuary, the inner house where God dwells. In Greek “you” is plural: the community together is the dwelling of God.
vv: For no one can lay any foundation other than the one that has been laid; that foundation is Jesus Christ.
Every bishop and priest, every catechist and parent, builds on a foundation he did not lay. The Lateran inscription honours the mother church, but the foundation even of the mother church is Christ.
Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you?
In the Old Testament the glory of God filled the Temple. Now the Spirit fills a people.
If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy that person. For God’s temple is holy, and you are that temple.

The same Greek verb is used twice, “destroy” and “will destroy”. In context Paul is thinking of those who tear the Church apart by division. To wound the unity of the Church is to damage God’s own house.
ch: The Catechism lists “the building of God” among the images of the Church and quotes this passage (CCC 756). It also teaches that the Holy Spirit is to the Church what the soul is to the body (CCC 797). St Augustine, preaching at the dedication of a church, told his people that what was done to these walls must be done in them: they too are being built, joined and dedicated (in substance).

r.h: The temple of his body
set: John places the cleansing of the Temple at the start of Jesus’ ministry, at the first of three Passovers in his Gospel. Matthew, Mark and Luke place it in the last week before the Passion. John puts it at the beginning like a heading over the whole Gospel: Jesus is the new Temple.

The Temple of Herod the Great was one of the wonders of the ancient world. Its outer courts held animal sellers and money changers, because pilgrims needed animals without blemish for sacrifice and the Temple tax had to be paid in a particular coin. The trade served the worship, but it had filled the house of prayer with the noise of a market.
str: vv. 13–16: at Passover, Jesus drives out the traders: “Stop making my Father’s house a marketplace!”
v. 17: the disciples remember Psalm 69.
vv. 18–20: the authorities ask for a sign; Jesus answers: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.”
vv. 21–22: the evangelist explains: he spoke of his body, and after the Resurrection the disciples believed.
kw: In vv. 14–15 John uses hieron, the whole Temple area with its courts. In vv. 19–21 he changes to naos, the sanctuary where God dwells. It is this naos that Jesus identifies with his body.
Jesus speaks as the Son in his Father’s house, not as a visitor. Zechariah had foretold a day when “there shall no longer be traders in the house of the Lord” (Zechariah 14:21).
The verb is used both for raising a building and for raising the dead. Jesus’ words carry both meanings.
vv: Stop making my Father’s house a marketplace!
His disciples remembered that it was written, “Zeal for your house will consume me.”
Psalm 69:9. In the psalm the righteous man suffers because of his love for God’s house. The disciples see that this zeal will cost Jesus his life.
Jesus answered them, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.”
The word “Jews” in vv. 18 and 20 refers, as often in John, to the Temple authorities who questioned Jesus, not to the Jewish people as such.
But he was speaking of the temple of his body.

The forty-six years of v. 20 fit the history: Herod began rebuilding the Temple about 20 BC, which places this Passover near AD 27–28. The stone Temple took decades; the new Temple is raised in three days.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus loved the Temple, went up to it for the feasts, and was angered that its outer court had become a place of trade; and that he identified himself with the Temple, presenting himself as God’s definitive dwelling among us (CCC 583–586). Through Christ the Church is “the temple of the Holy Spirit”, and the church building is the house where the people of God gather and Christ is present in the Eucharist (CCC 797, 1179–1181).

qa: Why does the whole Church celebrate a building in Rome?

The Lateran is the cathedral of the Bishop of Rome, the Pope. Keeping its dedication everywhere is a sign of love for and unity with the Chair of Peter. The feast is less about a building than about the one Church gathered around Christ and around Peter’s successor.
Was Jesus against the Temple?

No. Jesus was presented in the Temple as a child, found there at twelve, and went up for the feasts. He cleansed it because he loved it as his Father’s house (CCC 583–584). After the Resurrection the apostles continued to pray there (Acts 2:46; 3:1).
Was it right for Jesus to use a whip?

John says he made a whip of cords to drive out the sheep and cattle. It was a prophetic sign, like the actions of the prophets, done with authority and zeal for God’s honour. It does not justify violence against persons.
rite: The Lateran Basilica was given to the Church by the emperor Constantine, and tradition says it was dedicated by Pope Sylvester I on 9 November in the early fourth century. It was dedicated to Christ the Saviour, and later also to St John the Baptist and St John the Evangelist, which is why it is called St John Lateran. Its baptistery, built in the same age, became a model for baptisteries across the West. For Latin Catholics this day is also a lesson about our own parish church. At its dedication the bishop anointed the altar and the walls with chrism, marking twelve or four crosses, before which candles are lit on each anniversary. Every church building is a sign of the living Church, and every baptised person is a living stone.
study: Ezekiel’s river grows deeper the farther it flows. Where has God’s grace grown deeper in my life over the years?
Paul says the foundation is Christ and each builder must take care how he builds. What am I building on that foundation in my family or parish?
What “marketplace” noise do I need to drive out of my own heart so that it can be a house of prayer?
How can my parish show that it is united with the Pope and the universal Church?

lead: This week the first readings come from three short letters: Titus, Philemon and the second and third letters of John. Today Paul tells Titus how each group in a Christian household should live, and gives the reason: “the grace of God has appeared”. The Gospel balances this: when we have done everything, we are still servants who have only done our duty. Good works are the fruit of grace, not a claim on God.

r.h: The grace of God has appeared
set: Titus, a Gentile companion of Paul, was left in Crete to put the young Churches in order and appoint elders in every town (1:5). The letter is one of the three Pastoral Letters (with 1 and 2 Timothy). After warning against false teachers, Paul turns to what Titus must teach the members of the community.
str: vv. 1–8: teaching for older men, older women, young women, young men, and Titus himself as a model.
vv. 11–14: the reason for it all: God’s grace has appeared, trains us, and points us to Christ’s coming.
kw: Literally “healthy teaching”. True doctrine is meant to make a community well.
From the same root as “epiphany”: God’s grace has shown itself in the birth and life of Christ. In v. 13 the same root is used for his coming in glory.
The word for raising and educating a child. Grace does not only forgive; it teaches us how to live.
vv: For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to all
These verses are read at the Mass during the Night of Christmas. The grace that appeared in the manger is the same grace that shapes ordinary family life.
while we wait for the blessed hope and the manifestation of the glory of our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ.

In Greek one article governs both titles, and the most natural reading, which the NRSV follows, calls Jesus Christ himself “our great God and Savior”. The POC renders it as two names, “of our great God and of the Savior Jesus Christ”, which the Greek also allows. Many Fathers and modern scholars take the first reading, which makes this one of the clearest New Testament witnesses to the divinity of Christ.
ch: St Leo the Great, whose memorial is today, preached on Christmas Day: “Christian, recognise your dignity”, now that you share in the divine nature (CCC 1691). That is Paul’s argument to Titus: a new way of life follows from the grace that has appeared.

r.h: Only what we ought to have done
set: Jesus is on the road to Jerusalem. He has just told the apostles that even faith as small as a mustard seed can do great things (17:5–6). Now he guards them against a hidden danger: thinking that their service puts God in their debt.
str: vv. 7–9: a story from farm life: a servant who comes in from the field still serves his master first.
v. 10: the application: say, “We have done only what we ought to have done.”
kw: In Jesus’ world a servant belonged to his master’s household. The disciples are servants of God, and the apostles are their leaders.
The word means “of no extra profit”: they have given nothing beyond what was owed. It is a statement of humility, not of contempt.
vv: Do you thank the slave for doing what was commanded?
So you also, when you have done all that you were ordered to do, say, ‘We are worthless slaves; we have done only what we ought to have done!’
This is not the whole picture. Elsewhere Jesus says the master will put on an apron and serve his watchful servants himself (12:37). We cannot claim a reward; God gives it as a gift.
ch: The Catechism teaches that before God we have no strict right to any merit; our merits are themselves gifts of his grace (CCC 2007–2011). It closes that teaching with the words of St Thérèse of Lisieux, who wished to appear before God with empty hands, trusting in his love and not in her works.

qa: Does Luke 17:10 mean our good works do not matter?
No. Good works matter a great deal and God rewards them. But they are done by his grace, so we bring them to him as children, not as creditors.
rite: St Leo the Great was Pope from 440 to 461. His letter on the two natures of Christ, the Tome to Flavian, was read at the Council of Chalcedon in 451, and he went out in person to meet Attila the Hun in 452 to plead for Italy. He is a Doctor of the Church. His Christmas sermons echo today’s first reading.
study: Titus 2 gives teaching to old and young, men and women. Which part speaks most to my stage of life?
When do I expect God to owe me something for my prayers or my good works?

lead: Paul reminds Titus what Christians once were and what God has done: “he saved us … through the water of rebirth”. In the Gospel ten lepers are healed, but only one, a Samaritan, comes back to give thanks. Baptism and the Eucharist meet here: we are washed by mercy, and the right answer to mercy is thanksgiving.

r.h: The water of rebirth
set: Paul ends his instructions to Titus with how Christians should live in society: obedient to lawful authority, ready for good work, gentle to all. The reason is not social respectability but memory: we too were once lost, and God saved us by mercy.
str: vv. 1–2: conduct towards rulers and neighbours.
v. 3: what we once were.
vv. 4–7: what God did: a short hymn of salvation, naming the Father, Christ and the Holy Spirit.
kw: God’s love for humankind. Greek kings boasted of their philanthropy; Paul gives the title to God.
A clear reference to Baptism: a washing that gives new birth (compare John 3:5).
Those who receive an inheritance as children of the house. Baptism makes us heirs of eternal life.
vv: But when the goodness and loving kindness of God our Savior appeared,
he saved us, not because of any works of righteousness that we had done, but according to his mercy, through the water of rebirth and renewal by the Holy Spirit.
Salvation is pure mercy. Our works follow it; they do not buy it.
ch: The Catechism uses these words as one of the names of Baptism: “the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit” (CCC 1215). The whole Trinity is at work in vv. 4–7: the Father’s kindness, the Spirit poured out, through Jesus Christ our Savior.

r.h: The one who turned back
set: Jesus is travelling along the border between Samaria and Galilee. Lepers had to live apart and call out from a distance (Leviticus 13:45–46). Only a priest could declare them clean and allow them back into the community (Leviticus 14).
str: vv. 11–13: ten lepers cry for mercy from a distance.
v. 14: “Go and show yourselves to the priests”; on the way, they are made clean.
vv. 15–16: one turns back, praises God and falls at Jesus’ feet: a Samaritan.
vv. 17–19: Jesus’ questions and his word: “your faith has made you well.”
kw: A rare word. It is the word used on the stone notices in the Temple that forbade foreigners to go beyond the outer court. The one counted an outsider is the one who comes back to praise God.
The root of our word “Eucharist”. The Samaritan’s thanksgiving at Jesus’ feet is a picture of the Church’s worship.
vv: Then one of them, when he saw that he was healed, turned back, praising God with a loud voice.
All ten were cleansed; one saw. Seeing what God has done is the start of thanksgiving.
Then he said to him, “Get up and go on your way; your faith has made you well.”
The Greek verb also means “has saved you”. The nine were healed in body; the Samaritan received more.
ch: The Catechism teaches that every event and need can become an offering of thanksgiving (CCC 2638), and that the Eucharist is above all thanksgiving to the Father (CCC 1360). At Mass we are invited to be the one who turns back.

rite: St Martin of Tours (died 397) was a soldier and still a catechumen when, at Amiens, he cut his cloak in half for a freezing beggar. His biographer Sulpicius Severus tells that Christ appeared to him that night wearing the half cloak, and that Martin then asked for Baptism (in substance). He became a monk and then Bishop of Tours. Today’s two readings meet in his story: the water of rebirth, and a life of thankful love.
study: Titus 3:3 recalls what we were before grace. How does remembering my own past make me gentler with others?
For what healing in my life have I not yet turned back to give thanks?

lead: Paul writes a personal letter to ask a Christian master to receive his runaway slave as a brother. In the Gospel Jesus says that the kingdom of God is already “among you”, though the Son of Man must first suffer. Where Christ reigns, people who were divided are made brothers.

r.h: No longer as a slave but as a brother
set: Philemon was a Christian of Colossae in whose house the Church met (v. 2). His slave Onesimus had left him, perhaps after some loss or wrong (v. 18), and had come to Paul, who was in prison. There Onesimus became a Christian. Paul sends him back with this short letter, the most personal in the New Testament.
str: v. 7: thanks for Philemon’s love.
vv. 8–14: Paul appeals, not commands, for Onesimus his “child”.
vv. 15–17: receive him “no longer as a slave” but as a beloved brother.
vv. 18–20: “charge that to my account”.
kw: The name Onesimus means “useful”. Paul plays on it in v. 11: once useless to you, now useful to you and to me. In v. 20 he plays on it again: “let me have this benefit (onaimēn) from you”.
Literally the inner parts, the seat of deep feeling. It appears in vv. 7, 12 and 20: Paul sends Onesimus as “my own heart”.
vv: I am appealing to you for my child, Onesimus, whose father I have become during my imprisonment.
Paul fathered him in faith while in chains. The prisoner gives new life.
no longer as a slave but more than a slave, a beloved brother
Paul does not attack the law of the time directly; he places Philemon and Onesimus in a new relationship that makes the old one impossible to live in the same way.
If he has wronged you in any way, or owes you anything, charge that to my account.
Paul takes the debt on himself. Christians have long seen here a picture of Christ, who takes our debts on himself.
ch: The Catechism cites Philemon 16 when it teaches that it is a sin against human dignity to treat persons as merchandise or to enslave them (CCC 2414). The letter shows how the Gospel changes society from within: by changing the way brothers see each other.

r.h: The kingdom of God is among you
set: Some Pharisees ask Jesus when the kingdom of God will come. Many expected it with visible signs. Jesus answers them, and then speaks to his disciples about the day of the Son of Man.
str: vv. 20–21: the kingdom does not come with signs to be watched; it is among you.
vv. 22–24: do not run after rumours; the day of the Son of Man will be like lightning.
v. 25: but first he must suffer and be rejected.
kw: Watching closely for signs, as one watches the sky. The kingdom cannot be tracked like that.

The Greek can mean either. The NRSV and POC say “among you”: the kingdom is present in Jesus himself, standing in their midst. The Latin Vulgate has “within you”, and many spiritual writers read it of the inner life. Both are true, but the first fits the context best.
The word of divine necessity: the Son of Man “must” suffer. The way to glory passes through the Cross.
vv: For, in fact, the kingdom of God is among you.
But first he must endure much suffering and be rejected by this generation.
ch: The Catechism, explaining the Lord’s Prayer, recalls St Cyprian’s words that Christ himself may be called the kingdom of God, for in him we shall reign (CCC 2816). The kingdom is among us wherever Christ is present: in his word, in the sacraments and in the brother we receive.

qa: Why did Paul not tell Philemon to release all slaves?

Paul wrote within a society he could not change by one letter. But he put a seed into it: a slave is a brother “in the flesh and in the Lord”. Over time the Church came to teach clearly that slavery is contrary to human dignity (CCC 2414).
rite: St Josaphat Kuntsevych (1580–1623) was a monk and then Archbishop of Polotsk in the Ruthenian Church, which had entered into communion with Rome. He worked for the unity of the Church and was killed at Vitebsk in 1623. Like Paul in Philemon, he sought reconciliation; today we pray for unity among all Christians.
study: Is there someone I find hard to receive “as a brother” or sister? What would Paul say to me?
Where do I see the kingdom of God “among” us in my parish?

lead: The Elder warns a Church against teachers who deny that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh. Jesus warns his disciples that the day of the Son of Man will come suddenly, as in the days of Noah and Lot. Both readings ask us to stay with what is true and not to cling to what is passing.

r.h: Abide in the teaching
set: The second letter of John is the shortest book of the New Testament with the third. The writer calls himself “the elder”. He writes to “the elect lady and her children” (v. 1), most likely a local Church and its members. Some had left the community and were teaching a false idea of Christ (compare 1 John 2:19).
str: vv. 4–6: joy, and the old commandment: love one another, and walk in his commandments.
v. 7: deceivers who do not confess Jesus Christ come in the flesh.
vv. 8–9: be on guard; whoever abides in the teaching has the Father and the Son.
kw: The deceivers denied that the Son of God truly became man. The faith insists that the Word truly took our flesh.
Literally “going ahead”. The false teachers presented themselves as advanced. John says that whoever runs ahead of the teaching of Christ leaves God behind.
vv: And this is love, that we walk according to his commandments
Love and obedience are not two things. To love is to walk in his commandments, and his commandment is to love.
whoever abides in the teaching has both the Father and the Son.
ch: The Catechism notes that the first heresies denied not so much Christ’s divinity as his true humanity, against which the Church insisted that the Son of God came in the flesh (CCC 465). The Incarnation is the ground of our faith in the sacraments, where Christ still reaches us through bodily signs.

r.h: Remember Lot’s wife
set: Jesus continues his teaching on the day of the Son of Man (17:22–37). He draws on two stories from Genesis: the flood (Genesis 6–8) and the destruction of Sodom (Genesis 19).
str: vv. 26–30: in the days of Noah and of Lot, people went on with ordinary life until judgment came suddenly.
vv. 31–33: do not turn back; remember Lot’s wife; whoever tries to secure life will lose it.
vv. 34–35: one taken, the other left.
v. 37: “Where, Lord?” “Where the corpse is, there the vultures will gather.”

¶ The NRSV has no v. 36. A few manuscripts add “Two will be in the field; one will be taken and the other left” from Matthew 24:40, but the oldest do not have it. The POC numbers the verses without it, so its v. 36 is NRSV v. 37.
kw: Used of being taken along with someone. The saying stresses separation and suddenness, not a secret removal.
The word can mean either. The image is proverbial: the sign of death is plain to all. When the day comes, it will be unmistakable.
vv: Remember Lot’s wife.
She looked back at the burning city and became a pillar of salt (Genesis 19:26). Her heart stayed with what she was leaving.
Those who try to make their life secure will lose it, but those who lose their life will keep it.
ch: Eating, drinking, marrying and building are not sins. The danger is to live as if they were everything. The Catechism teaches that the Last Judgment will come when Christ returns in glory, and that only the Father knows the day and the hour (CCC 1040). The answer to that uncertainty is not fear but readiness.

qa: Does Luke 17:34–35 teach a secret “rapture”?
No. Jesus is describing the suddenness of his coming, which will separate people who seem alike outwardly. The Church teaches one glorious coming of Christ at the end (CCC 1038–1040).
study: What “Sodom” am I tempted to look back at with longing?
How can I keep the Incarnation, God truly in the flesh, at the heart of my faith?

lead: The Elder praises Gaius for welcoming travelling missionaries, so that “we may become co-workers with the truth”. Jesus tells the parable of a widow who keeps asking a judge for justice, to teach his disciples “to pray always and not to lose heart”. Hospitality and prayer are both ways of persevering.

r.h: Co-workers with the truth
set: The third letter of John is a personal note from “the elder” to Gaius. Travelling preachers moved from Church to Church and depended on local Christians for food and lodging. Gaius had welcomed them; a leader called Diotrephes had refused them (vv. 9–10).
str: vv. 5–6: Gaius has acted faithfully towards the brothers, even strangers; send them on in a way worthy of God.
vv. 7–8: they went out for the sake of the Name and took nothing from unbelievers; we ought to support them.
kw: for the sake of the Name
The Greek has simply “for the Name”, meaning the name of Jesus. The NRSV says “for the sake of Christ”; the POC keeps “for his Name”.
Those who receive missionaries share in their work. Hospitality is a form of mission.
vv: Beloved, you do faithfully whatever you do for the friends, even though they are strangers to you
Therefore we ought to support such people, so that we may become co-workers with the truth.
ch: The early Church organised such hospitality carefully; the Didache, an early Christian handbook, gives rules for receiving travelling apostles and prophets (in substance). Today the same work goes on when parishes support missionaries, seminarians and those who preach the Gospel far from home.

r.h: Pray always and do not lose heart
set: This parable follows Jesus’ words about the day of the Son of Man (17:22–37). While the disciples wait for his coming, they must pray. Luke states the point at the start: “their need to pray always and not to lose heart”.
str: v. 1: the purpose of the parable.
vv. 2–5: a judge who fears no one, and a widow who keeps coming.
vv. 6–8a: the lesson: if even this judge gives in, how much more will God grant justice to his chosen ones.
v. 8b: the question: will the Son of Man find faith on earth?
kw: To grow weary and give up. Prayer is the opposite of giving up.
Literally a boxing word, to strike under the eye. The judge jokes that the widow will “give him a black eye” by her persistence.
To vindicate, to defend someone’s rights. Widows had no one to defend them; God is their defender (Psalm 68:5).
vv: Then Jesus told them a parable about their need to pray always and not to lose heart.
And yet, when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on earth?
The parable ends with a question for us. The danger is not that God will fail to answer, but that we will stop asking.
ch: The Catechism names this among the parables of prayer that Luke records, together with the friend at midnight and the Pharisee and the tax collector (CCC 2613). It also teaches that we are to “pray constantly”, because prayer is the life of the new heart (CCC 2742–2745).

qa: Is God like the unjust judge?
No. The parable argues from the lesser to the greater. If even an unjust judge gives way to persistence, how much more will a loving Father hear his children.
study: Whom could I welcome or support, so as to become a co-worker with the truth?
In what prayer have I lost heart? What would it mean to keep coming, like the widow?

lead: On the Thirty-third Sunday in Ordinary Time, the second last Sunday of the Church's year, the readings look toward the end of all things and ask how we should live while we wait. The woman of Proverbs fills ordinary days with faithful work and opens her hand to the poor. Paul tells the Thessalonians that the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night, so the children of light keep awake. In the Gospel a master entrusts his property to his servants and, after a long time, returns to settle accounts. Psalm 128 sings of the blessing on those who fear the Lord and walk in his ways.

One thread runs through all three: something is entrusted, and there is a time of waiting before the account is given. The capable wife is trusted by her husband (Proverbs 31:11); the Thessalonians have received the faith and must not fall asleep; the servants receive the talents. Fear in the wrong sense makes the third servant bury his gift. The fear of the Lord, in the right sense, makes the gift grow. Since 2017 this Sunday is also the World Day of the Poor, and the readings fit it well: the gifts entrusted to us are meant to bear fruit, and the first fruit is mercy.

r.h: The woman who fears the Lord
set: Proverbs is a collection of Israel's wisdom, gathered over centuries and placed under the name of Solomon. The book ends with a poem of twenty-two verses (31:10–31) in praise of “a capable wife”. It is an acrostic: in Hebrew each verse begins with the next letter of the alphabet, from aleph to tav. The form itself says that this is praise from A to Z, a complete picture.

The book opened with Wisdom as a woman calling in the streets (Proverbs 1–9) and with the motto “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge” (1:7). It closes with a woman in whom wisdom has become daily life, and with the same fear of the Lord (31:30). So the poem is both a portrait of a real household and a picture of Wisdom herself living among people.
str: v. 10: the question: who can find such a woman? She is worth more than jewels.
vv. 11–12: her husband's trust; she does him good all her days.
v. 13: her work with wool and flax.
vv. 19–20: her hands at the spindle and, in the same breath, open to the poor.
vv. 30–31: the key: not charm or beauty but the fear of the Lord; let her works praise her in the gates.

¶ The lectionary leaves out the middle verses (trade, fields, a vineyard, clothing) but keeps the frame. Verses 19 and 20 are a pair in Hebrew: they use the two words for hand, yād and kap, in crossed order, and the same verb “to send out”. The hands that reach for the spindle are the hands that reach out to the needy.
kw: Ḥayil means strength, ability, even wealth or an army. The phrase could be rendered “a woman of strength” or “of worth”. Boaz uses the same words of Ruth (Ruth 3:11). The strength praised here is shown in work, wisdom and kindness.
Not terror but a reverent love that puts God first. It is the beginning of wisdom (Proverbs 1:7; 9:10), and the Church counts it among the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit (CCC 1831).
The word of Ecclesiastes, “vanity of vanities”: a breath, a vapour. In v. 30 beauty is called hebel. It passes like a breath; reverence for God lasts.
vv: A capable wife who can find? She is far more precious than jewels.
The question does not mean such women cannot be found. It means she is a gift, worth more than anything bought. Proverbs said the same of Wisdom: “She is more precious than jewels” (3:15).
She opens her hand to the poor, and reaches out her hands to the needy.
Her household is busy and prosperous, yet its door is open. Wisdom in Israel is never only private success; it includes care for the poor, the widow and the stranger.
Charm is deceitful, and beauty is vain, but a woman who fears the Lord is to be praised.
This is the key to the whole poem. Her skill, trade and strength all flow from one root: the fear of the Lord.
Give her a share in the fruit of her hands, and let her works praise her in the city gates.
The city gate was where the elders sat in judgment (v. 23). Her works speak for her in public. Here the poem meets the Gospel: the master too will look at what was done with what was entrusted.
ch: The Church reads this poem first as praise of real women and of the dignity of their work in the home and in society. St John Paul II, in his apostolic letter Mulieris Dignitatem (1988), speaks of the “perfect woman” of Proverbs 31:10 as an irreplaceable support and source of spiritual strength for others (n. 30). Christian commentators also read the poem spiritually: St Bede, in a short work on this chapter, saw in the strong woman the Church, the bride of Christ, who clothes and feeds her children (in substance). Placed beside the parable of the talents, she becomes a model of the good servant: faithful in small daily things, generous to the poor, and rooted in the fear of the Lord.

r.h: Children of the light do not sleep
set: This is very likely the oldest writing of the New Testament, sent by Paul from Corinth around AD 50–51 to a young Church he had been forced to leave in haste (Acts 17:1–10). The Thessalonians had questions about the end. In 4:13–18 Paul answered their grief over those who had died. Now he turns to the question of when: “the times and the seasons”.
str: vv. 1–2: no need to write about dates; the day will come like a thief in the night.
v. 3: the false peace of those who say “peace and security”, and the sudden labour pains.
vv. 4–5: but you are children of light and of the day.
v. 6: so let us keep awake and be sober.
kw: Chronos is time measured by the clock; kairos is the right or decisive moment. Jesus said the same before his Ascension: “It is not for you to know the times or periods” (Acts 1:7).
An old prophetic phrase for the day God acts in judgment and salvation (Amos 5:18; Joel 2:31). For Paul it is the day of Christ's coming.
Many scholars hear in this phrase an echo of Roman propaganda, which praised the peace and security of the empire. No human order can give the security that belongs to God alone.
The same verb Jesus uses: “Keep awake therefore” (Matthew 25:13). Christian watchfulness is not anxiety but alert, sober faith.
vv: For you yourselves know very well that the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night.
A thief does not announce his hour. The image comes from Jesus himself (Matthew 24:43; Luke 12:39). The point is readiness, not fear: the day will surprise the world, not those who are watching.
When they say, “There is peace and security,” then sudden destruction will come upon them, as labor pains come upon a pregnant woman
Labour pains are sudden, but they are not meaningless: they announce a birth. The end is both judgment and the birth of a new creation (compare Romans 8:22).
for you are all children of light and children of the day; we are not of the night or of darkness.
To be “children of” something is a Hebrew way of saying that we belong to it. Baptism, which early Christians such as St Justin called “illumination”, makes us children of the day.
So then let us not fall asleep as others do, but let us keep awake and be sober
ch: The Church has never fixed a date for the end, and she warns against those who do. The Catechism teaches that since the Ascension Christ's coming in glory is imminent, even though “it is not for you to know the times or periods” (CCC 673), and that we know neither the moment of the consummation of the earth nor the way the universe will be transformed (CCC 1048). Watchfulness, then, is a way of living each day as children of light. Paul's next verse names its armour: “the breastplate of faith and love, and for a helmet the hope of salvation” (5:8).

r.h: Enter into the joy of your master
set: This is the second of the three parables that close Jesus' last discourse in Matthew (chapters 24–25). The bridesmaids taught readiness; the talents teach faithful work during the waiting; the judgment of the nations (25:31–46) shows that the work is love for the least. Matthew wrote for a Church that had learned the master might be away “a long time” (v. 19).

A talent was not a coin but a weight of silver, worth about six thousand denarii. Since a denarius was a labourer's daily wage, one talent was the wages of many years, perhaps fifteen to twenty. Even the servant who received “only” one talent received a fortune. Our English word “talent”, meaning a natural gift, comes from this parable. Later Jewish law regarded burying money as the safest way to keep a deposit, so the third servant did what seemed prudent; the parable says that this caution was his failure.
str: vv. 14–15: the master entrusts his property, “to each according to his ability”, and goes away.
vv. 16–18: two servants trade at once; the third digs a hole.
v. 19: after a long time the master returns to settle accounts.
vv. 20–23: two reports and two identical words of praise.
vv. 24–27: the third servant and his fear; the master's reply.
vv. 28–30: the talent is taken and given; the worthless servant is cast out.
¶ The two faithful servants receive exactly the same words of praise, though one made five talents and the other two. What is rewarded is faithfulness, not the size of the result.
kw: A large weight of silver (see above). The amount shows how generous the master is.
From the same root as pistis, faith. The good servant can be trusted because he trusted his master.
The word suggests hesitating and shrinking back as much as idleness. Fear made the servant hold back.
“Enter into the joy of your master”: the reward is not only more responsibility but a share in the master's own happiness.
vv: to one he gave five talents, to another two, to another one, to each according to his ability.
The gifts differ, and that is not unjust. Each receives what he can carry, and each is trusted.
Well done, good and trustworthy slave; you have been trustworthy in a few things, I will put you in charge of many things; enter into the joy of your master.
Five talents are called “a few things”. Everything we receive in this life is small compared with what God wants to give.
so I was afraid, and I went and hid your talent in the ground. Here you have what is yours.

The servant's picture of his master (“a harsh man”, v. 24) is false. The false picture produces fear, and fear produces nothing. He hands back the gift unused, as if the relationship were only about not losing.
For to all those who have, more will be given, and they will have an abundance; but from those who have nothing, even what they have will be taken away.
This is not a rule of economics. In the life of grace a gift that is used grows, and a gift that is refused withers. Jesus said the same about hearing the word (13:12).
ch: The Fathers read the talents as all of God's gifts: natural abilities, the word of God, the grace of the sacraments. St John Chrysostom, preaching on this parable, said that the talents are whatever ability each one has, whether protection, money, teaching or anything else, and that whoever can help others and does not is like the man who buried his talent (in substance). St Gregory the Great saw in the five talents the gifts of the outward senses, in the two understanding and action, and warned that whoever has received understanding must use it to serve others (in substance). The Catechism teaches that talents are not distributed equally, so that each person needs others, and that these differences call for generosity, kindness and sharing (CCC 1936–1937). On the World Day of the Poor the parable has a plain meaning: what we have received, money, time, skill and faith, is given to be shared, and the next page of Matthew shows where the master expects to find its fruit: “just as you did it to one of the least of these who are members of my family, you did it to me” (25:40).

qa: Is God a “harsh man” who reaps where he did not sow?

No. That is the third servant's picture of his master, and the parable shows it to be false: the master gave lavishly and rewarded generously. He answers the servant on his own terms (“You knew, did you…?”) to show that even his excuse condemns him. Fear of a harsh God is the root of the buried talent; trust in a generous God makes the gift grow.
Does the parable praise making money or charging interest?

Jesus often took his images from ordinary life, here from business, but the subject is the kingdom of heaven. The point is fruitfulness, not finance. The Church's teaching on the just use of goods is found elsewhere, and on this very Sunday she asks us to share with the poor.
Who is the “capable wife” of Proverbs?

First of all a real wife and mother, honoured for wise and generous work. The poem also gathers up the whole book: she is wisdom made visible in a household. Christian readers have also seen in her a picture of the Church, the bride of Christ.
rite: In the Roman calendar this is the Thirty-third Sunday in Ordinary Time, the last before the Solemnity of Our Lord Jesus Christ, King of the Universe (22 November); Advent begins on 29 November. In these closing weeks the Church turns our eyes to the end of time and the return of Christ. Pope Francis instituted the World Day of the Poor in his apostolic letter Misericordia et Misera (2016) at the close of the Jubilee of Mercy, and set it on this Sunday, just before the feast of the King who will say, “you did it to me”. Many parishes share a meal with the poor, take up a collection or visit those in need. At Mass today the talent of the Gospel can take the shape of a hand opened, like the hand of the woman in Proverbs.
study: The woman of Proverbs is praised for faithful work in small, daily things. Which ordinary task of mine could become an act of the fear of the Lord?
Paul calls us “children of light”. What helps me to keep awake and sober in faith, and what lulls me to sleep?
What is the “talent” I am most tempted to bury, and what fear keeps it buried?
On the World Day of the Poor, what concrete step can my family or parish take this week to open our hand to the needy?

lead: In these last weeks of the year the weekday readings open the Book of Revelation. Today the risen Christ speaks to the churches of Asia and calls Ephesus back to the love it had at first. In the Gospel a blind beggar near Jericho cries out to the Son of David and receives his sight. Both readings are about seeing again: a Church that must remember what it has lost, and a man who prays, “Lord, let me see again.”

r.h: Remember the love you had at first
set: Revelation was written by a prophet named John, in exile on the island of Patmos “because of the word of God” (1:9), most likely near the end of the reign of the emperor Domitian (about AD 95), as St Irenaeus reports. It is addressed to seven churches in the Roman province of Asia, in today's western Turkey. Its style is apocalyptic: visions, numbers and symbols that show history as God sees it. It was meant to be read aloud in the liturgical assembly, and its first aim is to strengthen Christians under pressure, not to give a timetable of the end.
str: 1:1–3: the title, and the first blessing on those who read, hear and keep.
1:4: greeting from the eternal God, from the seven spirits, and from Jesus Christ.
2:1–5: the first of the seven letters, to Ephesus: praise (vv. 2–3), reproach (v. 4), a call to repent (v. 5).
kw: Not a riddle but the drawing back of a curtain. It is “the revelation of Jesus Christ”: given by him and about him.
1:3 is the first of seven beatitudes in Revelation. The blessing rests on those who hear the word in the assembly and keep it.
The love of the early days of conversion, warm and generous. Ephesus has kept sound teaching and endurance, but its love has cooled.
