Verse 5b is very difficult in Hebrew, and translations differ widely; the POC, for example, reads “Will we be saved?” But the sense of the whole is clear: the people stand before God with empty hands.
Yet, O Lord, you are our Father; we are the clay, and you are our potter; we are all the work of your hand.
The lament ends not in despair but in “Yet”. Our hope is not in our record but in who God is.
ch: The Catechism teaches that in Israel God is called Father because he is Creator and above all because of the covenant (CCC 238). It also explains why Advent reads such prophecies: when the Church celebrates Advent each year, she makes present the ancient expectation of the Messiah, so that by sharing in the long preparation for the Saviour's first coming the faithful renew their ardent desire for his second coming (CCC 524).

The Advent chant “Rorate caeli” sets the cry of the prophets to music, and the medieval hymn “O come, O come, Emmanuel” draws on the O antiphons sung at Vespers from 17 December. Both carry the longing of Isaiah 64.

r.h: As you wait for the revealing of our Lord
set: These are the opening verses of First Corinthians, written by Paul from Ephesus around AD 54. The Corinthian Church was gifted, lively and troubled: divided into factions, proud of its spiritual gifts, confused about the resurrection. Yet Paul begins not with rebuke but with thanksgiving. Before he corrects them, he reminds them of what God has given and what God will do.
str: v. 3: greeting: grace and peace.
vv. 4–6: thanksgiving for the grace given in Christ, rich in speech and knowledge.
v. 7: no gift is lacking as they wait for Christ's revealing.
v. 8: Christ will strengthen them to the end.
v. 9: God is faithful; he called them into the fellowship of his Son.
kw: A gift of grace (charis). Corinth valued the spectacular gifts; Paul will later say the greatest is love (13:13).
Christ's coming at the end is an unveiling: what is now hidden will be shown.
The prophets' “day of the Lord” (Amos 5:18) becomes the day of the Lord Jesus Christ.
Sharing in a common life. Paul uses the same word for the Eucharist: “a sharing in the blood of Christ” (10:16).
vv: so that you are not lacking in any spiritual gift as you wait for the revealing of our Lord Jesus Christ.
Christian life is lived between two comings. The gifts are given for the time of waiting.
He will also strengthen you to the end, so that you may be blameless on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.
The strength to persevere is not our own achievement but Christ's work in us.
God is faithful; by him you were called into the fellowship of his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord.
The whole letter rests on this sentence. The Corinthians were unfaithful in many ways, but God is faithful.
ch: The Catechism teaches that charisms are graces of the Holy Spirit oriented to the common good of the Church (CCC 799–800, 2003). This Sunday the Church hears Paul's thanksgiving as her own: she has been given everything she needs, the Word, the sacraments and the Spirit, while she waits for her Lord.

r.h: Keep awake
set: Mark 13 is Jesus' only long discourse in Mark, spoken on the Mount of Olives opposite the Temple (13:3). It speaks of the destruction of the Temple and of the end of the age. Jesus has just said that “about that day or hour no one knows” (13:32). Today's verses draw the conclusion: if the time is unknown, the only right response is to stay awake.
str: v. 33: “Beware, keep alert; for you do not know when the time will come.”
v. 34: the parable: a man goes on a journey, gives each servant his work, and orders the doorkeeper to watch.
vv. 35–36: you do not know when the master will come: evening, midnight, cockcrow or dawn.
v. 37: “What I say to you I say to all: Keep awake.”
kw: From the verb “to be awake”. The name Gregory comes from it. It is the key word of the passage, repeated three times.
Not ordinary clock time (chronos) but the decisive moment, God's appointed time.
The NRSV's “puts his slaves in charge” is literally “gives his servants authority, each his work”. Waiting is not idleness: each has a task.
The one who watches the door at night. Every Christian is a doorkeeper for the Lord's return.
vv: Beware, keep alert; for you do not know when the time will come.

A note on the text: many manuscripts add “and pray”, which the Latin Vulgate follows (“vigilate et orate”). The NRSV and the POC follow the manuscripts without it. Either way, prayer is the form watchfulness takes (14:38).
It is like a man going on a journey, when he leaves home and puts his slaves in charge, each with his work, and commands the doorkeeper to be on the watch.
The master is absent but has not abandoned his house. The time of his absence is the time of the Church.
for you do not know when the master of the house will come, in the evening, or at midnight, or at cockcrow, or at dawn,

These are the four Roman watches of the night. Mark's Passion follows the same night: the supper “when it was evening” (14:17), the disciples asleep in Gethsemane (14:37–41), Peter's denial at cockcrow (14:72), and Jesus handed over to Pilate “as soon as it was morning” (15:1). The disciples failed to keep awake that night.
And what I say to you I say to all: Keep awake.
The discourse was spoken privately to four disciples (13:3), but its last word is for everyone.
ch: The Catechism describes the present time as a time of waiting and watching, citing this passage (CCC 672). St Bernard, in a sermon read in the Office of Readings during the first week of Advent, speaks of three comings of the Lord: the first in the flesh and in weakness, the last in glory and majesty, and a hidden coming in between, in which he comes to us in spirit and power (in substance). Advent trains us for all three.

qa: Why does Advent begin with the end of the world, not with Christmas?

Because Advent has a twofold character. It prepares for Christmas, when we remember Christ's first coming, and it directs our minds to his second coming at the end of time (General Norms for the Liturgical Year 39). Until 16 December the second coming is in the foreground; from 17 to 24 December the readings prepare more directly for the Nativity.
Isaiah says “all our righteous deeds are like a filthy cloth”. Are good works worthless?

No. Isaiah speaks of a people's attempt to stand before God on their own record after turning away from him. The Church teaches that good works done in grace are truly pleasing to God, but that grace always comes first (CCC 2008, 2011). The point of the lament is that only God can save.
What does “tear open the heavens” have to do with Christmas?

Isaiah prays that God himself will come down. In Jesus that prayer is answered beyond all hope: God comes not with quaking mountains but as a child, and at the Jordan the heavens are torn open over him (Mark 1:10).
rite: Today the Latin Church begins a new liturgical year and a new Lectionary cycle, Year B, in which most Sunday Gospels come from Mark. The colour is violet, the Gloria is omitted until Christmas, and the Church's music and decoration are more restrained, so that the joy of Christmas may be fuller. In many homes and churches the first candle of the Advent wreath is lit today.

Advent begins on the Sunday falling on or closest to 30 November, the feast of St Andrew, which this year is tomorrow. The Collect of the day asks that we may run forth to meet Christ with righteous deeds at his coming.
study: Isaiah dares to say “Yet, O Lord, you are our Father” after confessing sin. Where in my life do I need to say “Yet”?
Paul thanks God for the Corinthians before he corrects them. How can I begin with thanksgiving in my family or parish this Advent?
Mark's four night watches return in the Passion. When have I been asleep at the moment Christ needed me to keep watch?
What one concrete practice will help me keep awake this Advent?

lead: On the feast of St Andrew the readings tell of a call and a sending. In Matthew, Jesus walks by the Sea of Galilee and calls two pairs of brothers, Andrew and Peter first, and “immediately they left their nets and followed him”. In Romans, Paul explains why such sending matters: people cannot call on the Lord unless they believe, cannot believe unless they hear, and cannot hear unless someone is sent. The psalm gives the verse Paul quotes: “Their voice has gone out through all the earth.”
Andrew is the first-called, and the one who brings others to Jesus. The key words of the day are calling, following and sending.

r.h: How beautiful are the feet
set: Romans 9–11 is Paul's long reflection, written with sorrow, on why many of his own people, Israel, have not yet accepted Jesus as Messiah, while Gentiles have. Chapter 10 says that salvation is open to all through faith in the Lord Jesus, “for there is no distinction between Jew and Greek”. Paul then asks how the message reaches people at all, and answers with a chain of questions. Chapter 11 will insist that God has not rejected his people (11:1–2).
str: vv. 9–10: confess with the lips, believe in the heart.
vv. 11–13: no distinction; everyone who calls on the Lord shall be saved (Joel 2:32).
vv. 14–15: the chain: call, believe, hear, proclaim, be sent; “how beautiful are the feet” (Isaiah 52:7).
vv. 16–17: not all obeyed (Isaiah 53:1); faith comes from what is heard.
v. 18: the message has gone out to all the earth (Psalm 19:4).
kw: To say the same thing, to agree publicly. Faith in the heart becomes a public confession.
Probably the earliest Christian creed. Kyrios is the word the Greek Old Testament uses for God's holy name. To call Jesus Lord is to confess his divinity.
The same word is used in v. 16 (“our message”) and v. 17 (“what is heard”). Faith is born from listening.
From this verb comes “apostle”, one who is sent. Andrew is honoured today as one of the Twelve whom Christ sent.
vv: because if you confess with your lips that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.
Lips and heart, confession and faith, belong together. The content is the heart of the Gospel: Jesus is Lord, and God raised him.
But how are they to call on one in whom they have not believed? And how are they to believe in one of whom they have never heard? And how are they to hear without someone to proclaim him?
How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news!
In Isaiah 52:7 these are the feet of the messenger running across the mountains to announce the end of exile. Paul applies them to the apostles.
So faith comes from what is heard, and what is heard comes through the word of Christ.
A note on the text: some manuscripts read “the word of God”. The oldest witnesses, followed by the NRSV, the Vulgate and the POC, read “of Christ”.
Their voice has gone out to all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.
Psalm 19 speaks of the heavens declaring God's glory without words. Paul applies it to the preaching of the Gospel, and so the Church sings this psalm on feasts of the apostles.
ch: The Catechism quotes Romans 10:14–15 to teach that no one, no individual and no community, can proclaim the Gospel to himself; the ministers of the Church are sent by Christ (CCC 875). It also teaches that by calling Jesus “Lord”, the first confessions of the Church's faith affirm that the honour due to God the Father is due also to Jesus (CCC 449). Pope St Paul VI wrote that the Church exists in order to evangelise (Evangelii Nuntiandi 14).

r.h: Immediately they left their nets
set: After his baptism and the temptations, Jesus moves to Capernaum on the shore of the Sea of Galilee, fulfilling Isaiah's promise of light for “Galilee of the Gentiles” (4:12–16). He begins to preach, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has come near” (4:17). His first act after that is to call disciples.

Fishing on the lake was hard work, often done at night, and it was a family business. Mark notes that Zebedee had hired men (Mark 1:20). John's Gospel adds that Andrew and Peter came from Bethsaida (John 1:44), and that Andrew had first been a disciple of John the Baptist and had met Jesus earlier in Judea (John 1:35–42).
str: vv. 18–20: Simon Peter and Andrew, casting a net; the call; they leave their nets.
vv. 21–22: James and John, mending nets with Zebedee; the call; they leave the boat and their father.
¶ The two scenes are told in the same pattern: Jesus sees, Jesus calls, they leave at once and follow. The pattern teaches every reader what a call looks like.
kw: Literally “come behind me”. The disciple's place is behind the master, walking where he walks.
In Jeremiah 16:16 God sends “many fishermen” to gather his people. The disciples' old trade becomes the image of their mission.
Matthew uses it in both scenes. The call of Jesus has an authority that makes delay seem unthinkable.
vv: he saw two brothers, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea

The net here (amphiblēstron) is a circular casting net, thrown by a man standing in the water or in a boat. Andrew stands beside his more famous brother; in the lists of the Twelve he is always among the first four.
Follow me, and I will make you fish for people.
Jesus does not ask them to stop being fishermen but to become a new kind of fisherman. Their skills of patience, teamwork and endurance are taken up into the mission.
Immediately they left their nets and followed him.
Immediately they left the boat and their father, and followed him.
The second pair leaves more: not only tools but family. The call reorders every bond, without abolishing love for parents.
ch: In the Gospel of John, Andrew is the first to follow Jesus and the first to bring someone else: he finds his brother Simon and says, “We have found the Messiah” (John 1:41). Later he brings the boy with five loaves (John 6:8–9) and, with Philip, brings some Greeks to Jesus (John 12:20–22). For this reason the Byzantine tradition calls him the Protoklētos, the First-called. Pope Benedict XVI, in a catechesis on St Andrew in 2006, noted that his name is Greek and saw him as a sign of the openness of the apostolic mission to the Greek world (in substance).
The Catechism teaches that Jesus chose the Twelve to be with him and to be sent out to preach (CCC 858), and that every vocation is a sharing in that mission.

qa: Did Andrew meet Jesus first in Judea (John 1) or in Galilee (Matthew 4)?

Both accounts can stand together. John tells of a first meeting near the Jordan, where Andrew, a disciple of the Baptist, spent a day with Jesus. Matthew tells of the decisive call some time later in Galilee, when Andrew left his work to follow Jesus for good.
Why is St Andrew pictured with an X-shaped cross?

An ancient tradition says that Andrew preached in Greece and was crucified at Patras in Achaia. The X-shaped cross (the saltire) comes from later medieval tradition. An old account of his martyrdom says that he greeted the cross with joy as the instrument of union with his Master (in substance).
Why is St Andrew important for Christian unity?

Andrew is the patron of the Church of Constantinople, as Peter is of Rome. Each year a delegation of the Holy See visits the Ecumenical Patriarch for the feast of St Andrew, and the Patriarchate sends a delegation to Rome for Sts Peter and Paul on 29 June. The two brothers pray together for their Churches.
rite: The feast of St Andrew stands at the doorway of Advent: the First Sunday of Advent falls on the Sunday nearest to this day. In Kerala, St Andrew's Basilica at Arthunkal in the Latin diocese of Alleppey is dedicated to him. Many Latin Catholics also begin today the popular “St Andrew Christmas Novena”, a short prayer repeated daily until Christmas, asking God to grant our requests through the merits of Jesus and his Blessed Mother. St Andrew teaches the Latin reader that the Advent hope is not kept to oneself: like Andrew, we bring others to Jesus.
study: Paul says faith comes from what is heard. Who first spoke to me of Christ, and to whom am I speaking of him?
Andrew and Peter left their nets “immediately”. What do I keep delaying in my response to Christ?
Andrew is always bringing someone to Jesus: his brother, a boy, some Greeks. Whom could I bring to Mass or to prayer this Advent?
How can our parish pray and work for the unity of Christians, as the feast of St Andrew invites?
